item.title: Real-Time Temperature Monitoring with Schneider Electric
item.description:
Source: Mouser

Turning Data into Action

In many industrial processes, temperature is a critical parameter that directly impacts product quality, equipment performance, and operational efficiency. Yet, many facilities still struggle with limited visibility into real-time process conditions, delayed responses to abnormal temperature variations, and insufficient local indications for operators. These challenges can lead to product losses, unexpected downtime, maintenance issues, and increased operational costs.

To address these pain points, Schneider Electric offers a simple, reliable, and scalable temperature monitoring and visualisation solution (Figure 1), enabling operators to monitor process temperatures in real time, receive immediate alerts, and react quickly before issues escalate. This blog explores how the solution integrates temperature sensing, signal conditioning, programmable logic controller (PLC)-based control, local visualization, and alarm indication into a unified architecture.

Figure 1: Full solution of Schneider’s real-time temperature monitoring system. (Schneider Electric)

Real-Time Industrial Temperature Monitoring Architecture

The temperature monitoring solution combines four complementary technologies into a single architecture.

Temperature Measurement and Signal Conditioning

At the core is an industrial temperature probe that continuously measures the process temperature. The signal is then processed by the Harmony Analog RMPT1UUBD temperature converter (Figure 2), which converts resistance temperature detector (RTD) signals into an isolated analogue output. In this implementation, the converter can be configured for a 0–10V output compatible with the TM221ME16T controller’s integrated analogue input suitable for industrial automation systems. Designed for flexibility, the converter supports multiple RTD sensor types, including Pt100, Pt1000, Cu50, and Cu100. Its ultra-compact design, integrated diagnostics, and simple dual in-line package (DIP)-switch configuration make installation and maintenance straightforward, even in space-constrained control panels.

Figure 2: Part of a range of analogue signal conditioners and transducers, the RMPT1UUBD targets applications interfacing RTDs to a current loop or as an output voltage. (Source: Schneider Electric)

PLC-Based Monitoring and Control

The conditioned signal is transmitted to the Modicon M221 logic controller (Figure 3), which serves as the system’s intelligence hub. The TM221ME16T controller acquires and processes temperature data in real time, manages alarm thresholds, and executes control logic to ensure reliable operation. Thanks to built-in Ethernet connectivity, serial communications, compact dimensions, and intuitive programming through SoMachine Basic, the Modicon M221 offers an efficient platform for machine-level automation and monitoring applications. Combining these multiple features into a single solution can also help reduce design costs. The controller’s flexible architecture allows designers to deploy standalone solutions today while remaining ready for future expansion.

Figure 3: Available in brick or book format, the M221 range of PLCs feature an embedded Ethernet port for easy integration into control system architectures. (Source: Schneider Electric)

Visual Status Indication and Operator Alerts

To improve operator awareness, the system integrates the Harmony XVTS smart tower light. Unlike conventional signalling devices, the XVTS1BSG (Figure 4) provides customisable RGB visual indication combined with an integrated audible alarm. Operators can instantly identify the status of a machine or process through configurable colour patterns and sound alerts. For example, the process temperature can be visualised through a colour gradient from cold blue to hot red. In this application, blue indicates a cold water temperature, while dark pink indicates the hottest value. This immediate visual feedback can help operators recognize changing process conditions and respond more quickly to configured alerts, which can help improve safety and minimise unplanned interruptions.

Figure 4: Tower lights like the XVTS1BSG offer smart features, including 9 to 15 customisable light segments, an optional buzzer, and dual operation via standard I/O. (Source: Schneider Electric)

Local Visualization and Operator Interaction

For local process visibility, the architecture also includes a href="https://eu.mouser.com/en/ProductDetail/Banner-Engineering/SD50P300WSQP?qs=bN4HulGPsrHsUh%252BCWKGTUQ%3D%3D">Banner Engineering SD50 display, which presents real-time temperature values directly at the machine level. Operators and maintenance teams can view real-time operating conditions, simplifying diagnostics and accelerating troubleshooting. For applications that require expanded data visualization and system interaction, a Schneider Electric human-machine interface (HMI) panel can be incorporated into the solution. (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Depending on the application’s needs, engineers can choose between an output-only LED display (SD50, left) and a full, customisable HMI with a touchscreen (Harmony STO & STU, right). (Source: Mouser)

Together, these technologies create a complete temperature monitoring solution that delivers continuous measurement, accurate signal conditioning, real-time processing, local visualisation, and proactive alarm management. The architecture is suitable for a wide range of industrial applications, including food and beverage production, water treatment, packaging machinery, HVAC systems, manufacturing equipment, chemical processes, and utilities.

Conclusion

A key advantage of this solution is the integration of Schneider Electric technologies within a unified architecture. Harmony Analog signal conditioning, Modicon M221 PLC control, Harmony XVTS visual indication, and local monitoring capabilities are designed to work seamlessly together, helping simplify system integration and deployment while providing a scalable foundation for future expansion. The combination of integrated components, real-time operational insight, and straightforward implementation helps organizations enhance process awareness, support informed decision-making, and respond more effectively to changing operating conditions.

 

Author Bio

With more than 15 years of experience at Schneider Electric, Guillaume Molinas has built extensive expertise in industrial automation, connected products, and Industry 4.0 technologies. Throughout his career, he has contributed to product development, industrial digitalization, technical support, and operational excellence initiatives. Today, as a Worldwide Level 3 Technical Support Expert for the Control & Signaling business, he provides advanced technical expertise on the Harmony connected ecosystem, supports global teams, and helps customers implement innovative connected solutions.

item.title: Machine Vision for Cobots and Industrial Sensors
item.description:
Machine vision pairs with conventional sensing to make cobots more flexible

Source: MstRowshanara/stock.adobe.com, generated with AI

Conventional automation performs well when each object arrives in a known position and the workspace stays consistent. However, when the consistency changes, a programmed movement can no longer suit the task. This challenge is being felt more in today’s automation environments as collaborative robots (cobots) enter applications where part placement, human activity, and working environments can constantly change.

A cobot can adjust if its control system receives enough information about what has changed. While confirmation that a part is present may be enough at a fixed loading point, this information provides less guidance when the part arrives in a different position or orientation. Therefore, machine vision adds information about the workspace to help cobot systems locate objects, identify visible features, and assess conditions before choosing their next action.

Our previous blog in this cobot series focused on the automation workflows that benefit most from cobot mobility. Here, we explore how machine vision differs from conventional sensing, how visual data enables cobots to adapt their motion, and the critical design challenges engineers must address when implementing these systems in production environments.

What Internal and External Sensors Tell the Cobot

Cobots already use many internal sensors to control their movement. But external sensors provide data about the surrounding environment and physical interaction. For example, a proximity sensor indicates whether an object has entered a defined range, while a photoelectric sensor detects an object through changes in received light.

Each sensor data point informs the cobot on a very specific aspect of position, presence, or contact. Cameras are also sensors, with imaging able to support several measurements across a scene. In the case of a 2D camera, it records light intensity and, with a color sensor, color information. Software analyzes this data to identify features and object position within the image plane.

3D vision systems add depth information. Software uses this information to estimate an object’s position and orientation in three-dimensional space. However, this estimate still depends on which surfaces are visible and how reliably the system measures them.

Simply adding more information does not make vision the best choice for every cobot. Sometimes, a proximity sensor can provide a more reliable presence check. Vision can estimate where contact should occur, but force sensing measures the actual interaction.

Therefore, complementary sensing assigns each method a clear role, where vision identifies and locates the object, internal feedback controls movement, contact sensors verify interaction, and safety-rated devices support protective functions.

Adaptive Navigation Uses Vision to Adapt the Robot’s Motion

In a scenario where different parts in an industrial factory are arriving at different positions and angles on a work surface, a fixed robot program expects each part at predetermined coordinates. If its placement changes, the programmed approach can miss the target. Vision enables the cobot to adjust its approach based on the observed position and orientation.

The workflow starts by capturing an image or 3D depth information. Next, software separates the objects from their backgrounds, identifies relevant features, and calculates the locations and orientations. A calibrated system converts this information into the robot’s coordinates.

For parts identified on a known plane, 2D vision can locate their position and planar rotation. Different characteristics like shape, color, labels, and edges can be useful for identification, while visible surface defects can be used for inspection. But when these parts vary in height, tilt, or overlap, 3D vision comes into play to add depth information required to understand the setup.

Furthermore, artificial intelligence (AI)-based vision can classify objects with variable appearances or identify features that are difficult to describe using fixed image-processing rules.

Designing the Vision System for Real-World Production Conditions

Designing a reliable vision system for cobots requires carefully accounting for environmental variables on the factory floor. In a real operating factory floor, changing ambient light, glare, reflections, and shadow can alter the features visible to the camera. For example, transparent surfaces may reveal the background while dark surfaces return little light.

Camera placement determines what information can be processed. A fixed camera provides a stable view of a larger workspace, but the robot or neighboring parts may create blind spots. Each measurement must be associated with the arm’s position at capture, using a calibrated relationship between the camera and the robot.

Selection starts with understanding the required field of view and working distance. These determine how much of the scene is covered and how many pixels represent a critical feature.

With a wider view at the same pixel count, the vision system reduces spatial detail. For 3D systems, depth accuracy needs to meet the task tolerance over the required range and production surfaces. Additionally, frame rates determine how often observations are available.

Image or depth data can improve feature detection, but it also increases bandwidth and latency requirements. For a moving object, delayed coordinates relay an earlier position. For example, at 0.5m/s, a 40ms delay corresponds to 20mm of travel. In the case of stationary parts, processing delays still consume cycle time.

Ultimately, the complete sensing system should be selected from the information and accuracy the task requires. The most advanced camera adds value only when its capabilities resolve a relevant uncertainty under production conditions.

Conclusion

As working environments constantly change, leveraging the right mix of sensory data is critical for operational success. Adding cameras to the sensing design is not an either/or choice. Conventional sensors are effective for precise, limited measurements and vision provides the spatial and contextual information cobots need to handle variation. The strongest cobot systems support automated operations by combining vision with different internal sensors, depending on the task.

The last part of this cobot blog series will review the various end effectors and discuss the ideal applications for each within industrial environments.

item.title: New Tech Tuesdays: Combining HMI Processing and Real-Time Control on One MCU
item.description:
New Tech Tuesdays

Join Mouser's Technical Content team for a weekly look at all things interesting, new, and noteworthy for design engineers.

High-resolution displays are common in everyday life, being integrated into applications ranging from medical and industrial equipment to consumer appliances. As these human-machine interfaces (HMIs) become more sophisticated, they increasingly combine displays, touch controls, voice interaction, and local data processing. While these advancing features give users a better experience, the equipment controlled by these interfaces still needs to perform its primary functions reliably and respond to events in real time.

What is changing amid this evolution is how much of the work a microcontroller unit (MCU) can handle by itself. GHz-class processing, vector acceleration, larger amounts of on-chip memory, and multicore architectures are expanding how much HMI processing, local analytics, and real-time control designers can handle on a single MCU.

Combining these requirements can make embedded systems more complex. Designers need enough processing performance for graphics and data analysis while still maintaining deterministic control of sensors, motors, and other hardware. While previous generations of equipment might have required multiple processors or moving from an MCU to a more powerful application processor, newer, higher-performance MCUs are beginning to shift that boundary between functions.

This week’s New Tech Tuesdays reveals how advanced microcontrollers are blurring the lines with application processors, the architectural benefits of bringing more processing onto a single device, and how the latest MCU designs are transforming modern embedded systems.

Bringing More Processing onto the MCU

Traditionally, MCUs have been optimized for control. Integrating processing, memory, and peripherals has made them a good fit for applications that require predictable responses and direct interaction with hardware. Application processors support more compute-intensive workloads and feature-rich operating systems such as Linux, while MCUs are designed around embedded control and deterministic response.

As embedded HMIs have become more capable, the distinction between these two solutions has become less clear. Modern MCUs can combine GHz-class processing with large amounts of embedded memory in hardware designed to accelerate demanding workloads.

Some of the extra processing power goes toward jobs that once needed additional hardware. For example, audio and sensor data involve repetitive calculations that vector processing can handle efficiently. The same hardware is also useful for machine learning (ML) workloads, such as voice recognition and equipment monitoring.

Multicore devices give designers another way to manage the competing demands. HMI processing might run on one core, while the other responds to sensors or controls a motor. Separating those jobs helps prevent a busy interface or processing task from interfering with tasks that need predictable timing. Meanwhile, keeping more functions on one device can reduce the number of components on the board and how much communication is needed between processors.

Combining workloads this way requires careful allocation of processing time, memory, and peripherals. The question for designers is becoming more about whether the HMI and local processing workload actually require a separate application processor.

The Newest Products for Your Newest Designs®

Renesas RA8M2 microcontrollers demonstrate how this new generation of high-performance MCUs can support greater integration. Built around a 1GHz Arm® Cortex®-M85 core, the RA8M2 provides the processing performance needed for demanding embedded applications while retaining an MCU architecture suited to real-time control.

The Cortex-M85 includes Arm Helium™ technology, providing vector processing capabilities that can accelerate digital signal processing (DSP) and ML workloads, enabling applications such as audio processing, local analytics, and other compute-intensive functions to operate alongside conventional embedded control tasks. Selected RA8M2 devices also include a 250MHz Cortex-M33 core, giving designers another way to partition workloads within the same MCU.

Large integrated memory further supports this approach. With up to 1MB of magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) and 2MB of static random-access memory (SRAM), the RA8M2 can accommodate application code and working data while reducing reliance on external memory. A parallel camera interface and a broad range of communications and peripheral interfaces also allow the MCU to connect directly with many of the devices used by modern embedded systems.

The RA8M2 is targeted at applications where designers need to combine responsive interfaces, connectivity, and local processing while still handling the real-time control expected from an MCU.

Tuesday’s Takeaway

As advanced microcontrollers continue to transform embedded system architecture, high-performance MCUs are changing where designers draw the line between an MCU and an application processor. As MCUs take on more HMI and data-processing work, designers have more options for keeping those functions alongside real-time control. In some systems, that means an MCU may now be enough.

item.title: Bringing Sensor Intelligence to Legacy Industrial Machines
item.description:
How connectivity, motor monitoring, and vision inspection add capabilities to legacy industrial equipment.

Source: Ahmed/stock.adobe.com, generated with AI

Industrial machines often remain mechanically reliable for decades but, over time, provide very limited information about their current operating condition and performance. Operators may believe that production is continuing normally even when they lack sufficient information to detect developing equipment issues or declining performance.

Replacing legacy industrial equipment can be difficult to justify when the production process continues to operate effectively. Beyond the capital expenditure, replacement comes with downtime, installation, and commissioning before production can resume.

Brownfield modernization adds capabilities to existing industrial equipment and infrastructure. When appropriate automation technologies are implemented, engineers can address specific operational limitations while retaining valuable assets.

In the first part of this blog series on updating brownfield operations, we examine three practical retrofit approaches: connecting isolated machines, monitoring motors, and adding vision inspection to production lines. Other options include energy monitoring, human-machine interface (HMI) upgrades, and asset tracking, but these three practical approaches demonstrate how manufacturers can improve visibility into machine operation, equipment condition, and product quality.

Data Access Paths That Fit Existing Infrastructure

Production counts can track output, but fault information explains why a cycle stopped. If the question is whether a shaft is rotating, a motor run command only shows that the controller requested movement. Each requirement calls for information that answers the question at the necessary update rate.

Choosing a data access method starts with understanding what the manufacturer needs to know about the machine.

Some of this information may already be stored in the programmable logic controller (PLC), machine controller, or installed instruments, even when the equipment is disconnected from plant information systems. Before using these values, engineers need to understand their source and what they represent. This includes verifying how a measurement is converted to engineering units and whether it updates frequently enough for the intended application.

A supported controller interface can provide this information, and a compatible gateway can provide access when the installed equipment uses an older interface. However, a gateway only makes existing data accessible. Additional sensing can help when the required measurement is unavailable.

The controller requires checking interface support, documentation, available communication capacity, and the polling frequency. Even read requests consume resources. Requesting information too frequently can affect controller performance. Engineers should acquire only the necessary information at a rate suited to the application.

Commissioning should confirm that measured values align with observed machine conditions. Other factors that influence the choice include installation costs, permitted network access, cybersecurity exposure, commissioning time, and recovery arrangements.

Engineers should choose the least intrusive access method that provides adequate information for the intended application.

Match Motor Monitoring to the Behavior Needing Detection

Monitoring vibration and temperature helps maintenance teams identify changes in equipment condition that might otherwise go unnoticed. But adding these measurements to existing industrial machines can provide earlier indication of potential problems without replacing the equipment or its control system.

Let’s suppose an existing motor driving a centrifugal pump that maintenance teams inspect periodically.

Adding monitoring solutions starts with the behavior to be observed. If the concern is a change in bearing vibration, an accelerometer mounted near the bearing housing can provide relevant information, while a temperature sensor can track heating at that location. These measurements offer different views of the pump. A change in any one does not necessarily indicate deterioration.

The usefulness of these measurements depends heavily on how they are installed. For example, an accelerometer attached to a loose cover may not capture the actual bearing housing vibration. However, a stiff mounting will improve mechanical coupling, and consistent thermal contact will help a temperature sensor follow the measured surface.

How the data is collected also depends on the behavior being observed. To capture rapid vibration, the sensor and acquisition system need enough bandwidth and sampling rate. Anti-alias filtering prevents higher-frequency signals from appearing as false lower-frequency components in the recorded data. If the system retains only an overall vibration metric, the original time waveform and most of the frequency-domain detail are unavailable for later analysis.

After installation, engineers need to establish how measurements vary under normal operating conditions. Baselines should include representative speeds and loads, as these conditions can affect readings even when the machine has not deteriorated. Startup and idle measurements should be treated separately from steady-state operation.

More advanced analysis becomes useful when the installation provides reliable evidence of abnormal behavior.

Fit Vision Inspection Into the Existing Constraints

Adding machine vision to an existing production line enables manufacturers to automate quality checks. For example, a camera captures an image, inspection software analyzes it against specified criteria, and the result can then be sent to an existing control system to identify or reject defective products.

For an existing industrial packaging line where a camera will check for label presence and read an identification code, the inspection task determines where the camera should be integrated and what it needs to see. The field of view needs to cover the label position and retain sufficient image detail to read the code.

Lighting is an important aspect of the vision system. Available mounting space and working conditions can constrain this arrangement. For example, a camera mounted on a vibrating guard moves relative to the product, and inconsistent part presentation can place labels outside the focus range. Therefore, the camera and light require stable mounts.

When the relevant part reaches the inspection position, the camera should capture the feature before movement blurs the image. While the part sensor triggers the capture, a short exposure can limit how far the product moves during capture because shorter exposure reduces the light collected.

The inspection result should be integrated with the existing controls. If a reject mechanism sits downstream, the controls need to follow that part from inspection to rejection and allow time for the mechanism to respond. Encoder feedback can help coordinate this action with conveyor travel when speed changes.

Commissioning should confirm that this sequence works through line speed changes, lighting variation, unreadable codes, and missing results.

Conclusion

A brownfield upgrade should begin with the operational uncertainty the manufacturer needs to resolve. Once that question is clear, engineers can select a capability that provides reliable evidence while working within existing infrastructure constraints.

The retrofit should leave operators and maintenance teams with equipment they can understand, verify, and maintain as part of their everyday operations.

In the next part of this blog series, we examine practical examples of how machine data can support brownfield modernization efforts.

item.title: How ERVs Improve HVAC Efficiency and Indoor Air Quality
item.description:
Source: Evgenii Bakhchev/stock.adobe.com

Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems play a critical role in maintaining clean, comfortable commercial spaces and meeting indoor air quality (IAQ) requirements. Because HVAC equipment often operates for extended periods during hot and cold seasons, energy efficiency remains a key design consideration. Energy recovery ventilators (ERVs) support mechanical ventilation also known as DOAS (Dedicated Outdoor Air System) by supplying outdoor air and exhausting indoor air while using the outgoing airstream to precondition the incoming air’s temperature and moisture content. By reducing the load on heating and cooling equipment, ERVs can significantly improve overall HVAC efficiency. However, achieving these benefits requires careful system design, control, and maintenance.

This blog examines how ERVs enhance IAQ and HVAC efficiency and explains the role of airflow and pressure sensing in maintaining efficient operation.

Understanding ERVs in Commercial HVAC Systems

Indoor commercial environments can accumulate carbon dioxide (CO2), airborne particulates, and gaseous contaminants that degrade occupant comfort, health, and well-being. To maintain acceptable IAQ, ventilation systems must continuously introduce outdoor air while removing stale indoor air. Standards such as ASHRAE 62.1 with their VRP (Ventilation Rate Procedure) procedure set minimum ventilation requirements for commercial buildings, with required ventilation rates varying by factors such as space type, building area, and occupancy levels.[1]

How ERVs Reduce HVAC/DOAS Energy Demand

To meet ventilation requirements, HVAC systems use the demand controlled ventilation (DCV) control strategy to continuously manage airflow as building conditions and occupancy levels change. As a result, many commercial HVAC systems incorporate variable air volume (VAV) systems to monitor and maintain appropriate ventilation rates.

HVAC systems must bring sufficient outdoor air into buildings as conditions and occupancy levels change to meet ventilation requirements, but doing so can create additional challenges. Depending on ambient conditions, incoming air may require heating, cooling, humidification, or dehumidification before it can be supplied to occupied spaces. This continuous conditioning increases HVAC energy consumption and operating costs and can also increase demand on mechanical components such as fans, pumps, and compressors. ERVs can help reduce this load by recovering energy from conditioned air as it is exhausted from the building.

ERVs use outgoing air to precondition fresh air entering from the outside. Inside an ERV, the incoming and outgoing air streams remain separate, but the system transfers energy between them before the indoor air is exhausted from the building. This allows the ERV to recover energy (heat) and latent energy, which is associated with moisture, rather than allowing the energy to leave with the exhaust air.

Energy recovery typically occurs through a rotating enthalpy wheel, a static plate, or a core-based recovery system. In an enthalpy wheel-based ERV, the wheel rotates between the supply and exhaust air streams, absorbing and releasing heat and moisture as it moves between them. The wheel typically contains a material (desiccant) capable of absorbing the humidity in the wet airstream and releasing it in the dry airstream. Static systems keep the two air streams in separate channels within a fixed core, and heat and moisture are transferred through the material separating them. Regardless of the design, the goal is to moderate the temperature and humidity of incoming outdoor air before the HVAC system completes conditioning it.[2]

Energy transfer varies by season. In winter, warm indoor exhaust air transfers heat to the cold, dry outdoor air entering the building. The incoming air is warmer and, in an ERV that transfers moisture, it's also more humid before it reaches the HVAC system. In summer, cooler indoor exhaust air absorbs heat and moisture from the hot, humid outdoor air, so the incoming air is cooler and drier.

The ERV does not replace the HVAC system or even bring incoming air to the desired indoor temperature and humidity. Instead, it reduces the heating, cooling, humidification, and dehumidification required. The preconditioned outdoor air can then be further conditioned by the HVAC distributed through the building’s ductwork.

Maintaining ERV Performance Through Pressure Sensing

For ERVs to operate efficiently, the fans that move air in and out of the ERV housing and heat exchangers must be precisely controlled. This is because the air entering and exiting the ERV must have the proper airflow for the heat exchangers to operate at peak efficiency and achieve the desired air temperature and humidity exchange rates. The indoor and outdoor air temperatures, humidity levels, filter conditions, building occupancy levels, and main HVAC system operation all affect the air conditions for ERVs. Using a differential pressure sensor in an ERV blower control system enables the system to adapt to changes in these conditions with adequate response time to ensure efficient operation. By directly measuring the airflow by methods like a Bernoulli ring at the blower or Pitot Tube in the airduct or inside the ERV the EC motor driving the blower can be controlled to deliver the exact amount of air needed. In comparison to RPM and current based air volume control, true airflow is more accurate, failsafe and precise.

One example of such a sensor is Sensirion’s SDP8xx Digital and Analog Pressure Sensors, which are designed to accurately measure air pressure in high-volume applications without offset drift. These sensors cover typical air-pressure ranges for commercial applications and provide rapid response times for real-time control. The performance advantages of these sensors are enabled by Sensirion's patented CMOSens® sensor technology, which integrates the sensing element, digital calibration, signal processing, and analog output on a compact CMOS chip that is fully calibrated, temperature-compensated, and offers outstanding long-term stability.

High-quality, reliable monitoring of airflow at the ERV’s inputs, outputs, and internal components enables optimized fan speeds in response to changing conditions. With good data collection practices and intelligent control system design, pressure measurements can also reveal trends in ERV operation that indicate the need for service or maintenance. For example, as filters accumulate dirt, the resulting change in pressure can help indicate when they need to be replaced.

Conclusion

Accurate airflow play a key role in maximizing ERV energy efficiency. By transferring heat and moisture between exhaust and incoming air streams, ERVs help maintain indoor air quality while reducing DOAS HVAC energy consumption. Differential pressure sensors support this process by providing the feedback needed to optimize fan operation.

item.title: How Industrial Automation Teams Reduce Commissioning Risk
item.description:
Source: Andrey Popov/stock.adobe.com

When an automation project runs into trouble during commissioning, the first instinct is usually to look at the controls: the logic, sequencing, I/O, wiring, drive behavior, network configuration, or software. That instinct makes sense—controls are tangible, testable, and present when the problem appears. But in practice, many commissioning issues blamed on control engineering actually originate much earlier.

This blog explores how experienced industrial automation teams reduce commissioning risk by proving key assumptions early, designing for support, aligning operational technology (OT) and information technology (IT), and preparing operators before the project ships.

Reducing Risk Before Commissioning

I started as a programmer at B&R Industrial Automation, now part of ABB, and spent more than 24 years moving between technical and management roles across the industrial automation ecosystem. Technical execution matters enormously.

In my experience, many project outcomes are shaped long before commissioning begins. The teams that consistently deliver successful projects are not necessarily those with the strongest control engineers. More often, they are the teams that got the coordination right early, surfaced risks while they were still inexpensive to address, and designed beyond the narrow goal of “passing startup.”

By the time a technician is troubleshooting on the floor, the controls often reveal only a problem that started months earlier: an assumption that was never documented, a tradeoff that was never confirmed with the people affected, or an agreement that existed only at one level of the organization. When the coordination tasks are executed effectively, commissioning is mostly a verification exercise. When it is not, commissioning turns into discovery, and discovery at that stage is typically more expensive because it adds field labor, rework, production delay, and prolonged stabilization on top of the engineering effort already invested.

I learned this lesson early in my career. At a project kickoff, we discussed having a machine “running by summer”. Within the engineering group, that meant the motion layer: axes tuned, movements verified, and a stable platform ready for application code. To the customer, however, it meant something closer to a first usable version of the machine, with sequences implemented and the process functioning in a recognizable way.

Both interpretations were reasonable, and both groups spent months believing the project was on track. The gap surfaced only when the schedule tightened, and expectations were compared directly. What looked like an engineering delay turned out to be a coordination failure that had started in the very first conversation. The phrase "machine running" had meant two different things to two groups of professionals, and nobody had made either interpretation explicit.

The cost was real. The engineering team faced the consequences of a misunderstanding that was not their fault. The schedule had not slipped because the work was poorly executed. It slipped because the milestone meant different things to different people, and that was never made concrete while it was still cheap to fix.

Small, aligned teams often resolve expectation mismatches and misunderstandings naturally through their day-to-day interactions. The person implementing the solution hears service concerns directly, while the person interacting with the customer understands the engineering team’s priorities and constraints. As a result, assumptions surface and are corrected while they are still easy to address.

Large projects tend to lose this advantage. Management talks to management, engineering talks to engineering, and operations enters the discussion later than it should. Everyone may leave a meeting believing there is alignment, but each group is carrying a slightly different version of the same decision. Nobody has to be careless for this to happen. The agreement exists at too high a level. Beneath it sit multiple versions of the same decision, each internally consistent and quietly incompatible. The challenge in a large project is to deliberately create the shared understanding that small teams develop naturally through everyday interactions. In my experience, four areas make the greatest difference in preventing misalignment across project teams and reducing risk before commissioning even begins:

  1. Strategic governance
  2. Operational continuity
  3. Technical resilience
  4. Adoption and sustainment

Strategic Governance: Prove the Right Things Early

The first area is strategic governance. The teams that handle strategic governance well start every project with an honest accounting of what they do not yet know. Not what they need to build, but what they need to prove. These are different questions, and failing to distinguish between them is one of the most common causes of late-stage rework. For most projects, the unknowns that matter most are the ones where being wrong is most expensive: new process behavior, unproven control strategies, integration constraints, and throughput assumptions. When one of these turns out to be wrong late in the project, the fix usually requires revisiting decisions that the rest of the work was already built around. A shared list of what the team must prove, in priority order, makes those unknowns visible early and forces a clearer conversation about what is known and what is still being assumed.

The same discipline applies to planning for the Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) and the Site Acceptance Test (SAT). Well-run projects decide early what will be verified at FAT and what will be explicitly deferred to SAT or startup. That clarity prevents risk from quietly migrating downstream with the schedule while strengthening the supplier-customer relationship, because both sides agree on what “ready” means before testing begins.

When this step is skipped, the problems are predictable. A line may be mechanically complete before anyone proves the process can sustain the required throughput. A control sequence may work in simulation but fail when real device timing, network load, or the behavior of upstream and downstream equipment is introduced. These are not just technical misses. They are issues that could have been identified earlier but remained hidden until they became far more expensive to resolve.

Operational Continuity: Design for Support, Not Just for Testing

The second area is operational continuity. The teams that get operational continuity right bring service and maintenance into the design conversation early, not as reviewers but as sources of requirements. The service and maintenance questions that determine whether a machine is supportable must be addressed during design, because addressing them later usually means revisiting decisions already embedded in the system.

The operational continuity questions are specific. Can the machine be diagnosed remotely? Does the event history provide enough context to explain what caused a fault, not just that one occurred? Can maintenance isolate a problem in the human-machine interface (HMI) without contacting the original equipment manufacturer (OEM)? What will a technician see when something goes wrong, and will it guide them to the fault or merely indicate that something is wrong?

Mechanical teams usually ask these questions naturally. They consider access panels, replacement procedures, and component layout because those concerns are visible during design. In controls and software, the equivalent thinking is easier to skip precisely because the gaps remain invisible until the machine is in production.

The economics make early engagement worthwhile. Up to the point when the machine leaves the facility, mistakes primarily cost engineering time. After that, they can lead to production downtime, emergency support, site visits, and lost customer trust.

A machine that passes every functional test can still generate excessive support calls if the diagnostic pathway is unclear. The operator sees one alarm, maintenance sees a different symptom, and support receives a description based largely on guesswork. At that point, a seemingly minor design decision becomes an ongoing operational cost.

Technical Resilience: Align OT and IT Before the Architecture Is Fixed

The third area is technical resilience. Teams that manage it well treat OT and IT alignment as a design requirement rather than an integration task. They bring the right people from both sides into the same conversation before architecture choices are finalized, because the cost of misalignment rises sharply once those choices are locked in.

OT teams optimize for uptime and recoverability, while IT teams optimize for control, security, and manageability. These perspectives are not incompatible, but they lead to different architectural choices when developed in isolation.

When an OT team designs around a flat network topology for fast recovery and IT enters the conversation only after the architecture is committed, the machine may still be commissioned on time. But if segmentation is then required for security compliance, reliable software updates to field controllers can take months to resolve after handoff. The system worked at commissioning, but it becomes harder to update, secure, and support over its operating life.

From a project standpoint, the requirement is straightforward: the system must be updatable, diagnosable, and supportable after deployment, not just functional at commissioning. This means version control, configuration baselines, diagnostic logging, and audit trails must be treated as design requirements from the start, not as documentation tasks at the end.

The practical shift is to treat OT/IT alignment as a project deliverable alongside the controls work, with clear owners and explicit readiness criteria, rather than leaving it to the two sides to resolve after the architecture is finalized.

Adoption and Sustainment: Prepare the Handoff Before the Project Team Leaves

The final area is adoption and sustainment. Well-run projects plan for operational handoff long before commissioning. The people who will run and maintain the system are part of the conversation before the design is finalized. Training focuses on the failure conditions most likely to occur in the field, not just on normal operation. Documentation reflects the software version that was actually released. Alarm messages provide the context a technician needs to act, not just a fault code.

The standard for holding the project to is not simply “does the machine work?” but “can the people responsible for it run it, troubleshoot it, and recover from failures without calling the project team?” These are different questions, and delivery pressure reliably leads teams to answer only the first.

In practice, the things that matter most here are often unglamorous: consistent alarm classes that help operators and maintenance personnel assess urgency, fault presentation that guides a technician to the problem rather than simply indicating that something is wrong, naming conventions that match what operators see on screen, and displays that provide enough context for technicians to understand the machine’s state without having to make a phone call. None of these are technically difficult. They become expensive only when treated as finishing details rather than as design requirements.

What Needs to Be in Place Early

What helps most is usually simpler than teams expect, and most of it can be set up at the start of the project.

The single most useful habit is to write down assumptions. Every project runs on assumptions that everyone believes, but no one has documented. A shared list, with an owner and a review date for each item, makes them visible before they harden into commitments. It also shows that, while the cost of acting is still low, some beliefs are well-founded while others have never really been tested.

The same discipline applied to decisions helps just as much. A brief record of what was decided, by whom, and what must remain true for it to hold prevents those decisions from being quietly re-litigated as people change or the project evolves.

Two practices are especially worth establishing from the start because teams often leave them too late. The first is the test specification. Early in my career, our team shipped a new software version for a machine. We had done real engineering work: updates, feature changes, and improvements. Then the machine would not start. Not figuratively. The start button did not work. We were focused on what had changed and lacked a test specification that forced us to verify the most fundamental expected behavior first. Something everybody knows is often the very thing nobody explicitly checks. That experience is why the test specification matters.

A test specification should start with the most fundamental expected machine behavior: the start button, the stop command, and the basic cycle, then build outward from there. Not because advanced behavior does not matter, but because basic behavior is exactly what everyone assumes has already been verified, even when it has not.

The second is traceability. Before the machine goes to the site, the team should be able to clearly state which software version is running, which configuration was deployed, and what diagnostic data will be available if something goes wrong in the field. If those answers require a search, field support will rely on guesswork rather than on evidence.

The Goal Is to Surface Risk Early

This approach is not about replacing engineering with process. It is about equipping engineers, operators, service teams, and customers with the information they need to make good decisions while keeping the cost of those decisions manageable.

Every project runs on assumptions. What usually separates a manageable project from a painful one is when those assumptions are tested.

Found early, there are tradeoffs.

Found at commissioning, they are reworked.

Found in production, they become a cost, a delay, and a support burden.

The projects that go well are not the most formally managed or the best documented. They are the ones where the right people talk to each other early, before designs are finalized, before commitments are made, and before the machine leaves the building.

That is how a large automation project begins to operate more like a small, aligned team. The useful question on every project is not just what might go wrong at commissioning, but what needs to be known early enough to keep the project on track.

item.title: New Tech Tuesdays: Hydrogen Sensing Gives Battery Packs an Earlier Warning Signal
item.description:
New Tech Tuesdays

Join Mouser's Technical Content team for a weekly look at all things interesting, new, and noteworthy for design engineers.

As electric vehicles (EVs), battery energy storage systems (BESS), industrial backup systems, and high-power charging platforms continue to scale, the battery pack is becoming a more active, sensor-rich environment. The goal of battery management is not only to manage charge and discharge, but also to recognize abnormal cell behavior before it becomes a larger system-level event.

That is where early hydrogen-based thermal runaway detection is gaining attention. During certain lithium-ion cell failure conditions, gas generation can occur before a dramatic temperature rise or visible pack damage. Detecting hydrogen near the cell level gives designers another early warning indicator to pair with temperature, pressure, voltage, and current monitoring data.

In this week’s New Tech Tuesdays, we look at how hydrogen sensing is becoming part of the battery safety conversation, why the technology is moving closer to the cell, and how compact gas sensors can help engineers design safer EV and BESS packs.

The Need for Earlier Battery Fault Detection

As EV and BESS designs move into more demanding operating environments, robust failure detection becomes increasingly critical. Vehicle packs must handle vibration, rapid load changes, fast charging, and wide temperature swings. Stationary storage systems may operate for years in outdoor cabinets, renewable-energy installations, or grid-support environments where maintenance access can be limited.

Legacy battery pack monitoring systems primarily monitor electrical and thermal signals. But as cell density increases, the time it takes for a localized fault to become a system-level failure shortens. As a result, battery designers need early-warning systems that can identify potential faults even before electrical and thermal warnings are triggered.

Stressed lithium-ion batteries begin off-gassing hydrogen and other gases as their internal pressure rises. Because ambient hydrogen concentrations are normally very low, a significant hydrogen increase within a battery enclosure can provide a useful fault indicator. Detection reliability, nevertheless, depends on sensor selectivity, environmental compensation, sensor placement, alarm thresholds, and potential hydrogen sources in the surrounding system.[1] When integrated with an appropriate safety system, hydrogen detection can trigger actions such as current interruption, pack isolation, ventilation, cooling, or an external warning before the event progresses further.

Enhancing Fault Detection Systems with Hydrogen Sensing

The next stage of battery safety will likely involve more sensor fusion. As this evolution takes shape, hydrogen detection will not replace monitoring of temperature, humidity, pressure, voltage, or current. Instead, it can give the system another independent signal that strengthens decision-making. A hydrogen rise near a module vent, combined with an unusual temperature gradient or voltage deviation, can provide more confidence than any single measurement alone.

For both EVs and BESS, early gas detection can become part of a layered safety approach that includes cell chemistry, mechanical spacing, thermal barriers, venting, power electronics, and system-level controls.

The Newest Products for Your Newest Designs®

As hydrogen detection becomes an important part of layered battery safety, the Sensirion STC42A Hydrogen Thermal Conductivity Sensor offers designers a compact solution for monitoring this early warning signal. Designed for early detection of hydrogen in battery environments, the STC42A gives engineers a compact sensing option for EV and BESS pack safety designs.

The STC42A is intended for applications where a thermal runaway warning must occur before a cell event grows into a broader pack-level issue. By focusing on hydrogen detection, the sensor can provide a signal that complements the electrical and thermal measurements already used in battery management systems. This feature makes it useful for designs that need to combine gas detection with temperature, and with humidity monitoring performed using a corresponding external humidity-and-temperature sensor, battery system diagnostics are able to offer significant safety enhancements.

The compact, low-power sensor uses proven sensor technology for high accuracy. With the sensor element, signal processing, digital calibration, and I2C communication on a single chip, the STC42A conveniently adds a layer of safety to battery designs. 

Tuesday’s Takeaway

Battery safety is evolving from simply monitoring temperature and electrical performance to incorporating a broader range of diagnostic signals. By adding hydrogen detection to the sensing toolkit, designers can strengthen layered safety strategies and help improve fault detection, system awareness, and overall safety in next-generation EV and BESS platforms operating in increasingly demanding environments.

item.title: Building Modular Machines with Cabinet-Free Distributed I/O Architecture
item.description:
Source: HumblePride/stock/adobe.com, generated with AI

Industrial machines have traditionally routed field-device wiring to input/output (I/O) modules and controllers housed in centralized control cabinets. As production systems become more modular, designers are increasingly placing selected I/O and control functions closer to the equipment they serve.

Traditional architectures often require long cable runs between field devices and the control cabinet, increasing installation complexity and making fault isolation more difficult. These designs can also limit flexibility when machine modules need to be added, removed, or relocated. Distributed architectures address these challenges by placing I/O closer to the equipment it services and routing communication with the control system over an industrial network.

This blog explores the key considerations for moving I/O out of the control cabinet and explains how rugged, modular I/O systems can help meet the environmental, connectivity, and reliability requirements of cabinet-free deployment.

The Engineering Design Challenge

In a traditional centralized architecture, machine components, including sensors and actuators, connect to terminal blocks and I/O modules in the control cabinet regardless of their location. This architecture works for simple plant layouts but becomes challenging as machine complexity and I/O points increase. Connecting every device to a central cabinet often results in extensive and complex wiring runs.

To reduce wiring complexity and support modular machine designs, engineers increasingly deploy distributed architectures. Distributed I/O places remote input and output modules near field devices while retaining a centralized or higher-level controller. A distributed-control architecture goes further by assigning control functions to controllers located at individual machines, stations, or production modules.

Moving I/O away from a central cabinet exposes the units to environmental conditions that the cabinet previously helped mitigate. These factors include dust and debris, moisture, vibration and mechanical shock, temperature variations, electromagnetic interference (EMI), and potential cable and connector damage. As a result, engineers need to evaluate each environmental condition when selecting hardware for the installation. Ingress protection (IP) ratings define specific levels of protection against solids and water. IP65 addresses dust ingress and water jets, while IP67 adds protection during temporary immersion under defined test conditions. The required rating depends on the application, and it applies only when the equipment is correctly assembled with the required seals, connectors, and closures.

Environmental protection is only part of the design challenge. Maintaining visibility for diagnostics and fault isolation remains critical even in distributed systems. Manufacturing environments require automation functions to be integrated without compromising safety, troubleshooting efficiency, or system availability.

Engineers must ensure that motor control hardware, I/O modules, and sensors operate together as a cohesive automation system, accounting for diagnostics to change potentially with new distributed configurations. Units need to be easily replaceable and must have clearly identifiable fault locations, preferably with wiring that does not have to be dismantled every time the electronic component is serviced.

While the flexibility to add different sensors, motors, or machines as requirements change is one of the many advantages of distributed architectures, it can easily lead to chaos if the process lacks standardization. Engineers need to work with a consistent blueprint for hardware architecture and maintenance to ensure work is verifiable and reproducible.

Technology Trends Meeting this Challenge

The shift toward distributed architectures reflects the growing demand for scalable automation and platforms that can adapt to changing production requirements. Modern manufacturing processes often consist of modular production stages that move workpieces between robotic systems, inspection stations, and packaging equipment. This modular approach benefits from keeping control and I/O functions closer to individual stations, simplifying commissioning and system integration. It also enables engineers to configure, monitor, and maintain these functions within a more unified automation environment rather than treating each station as a separate system.

At the same time, the availability of rugged, cabinet-free designs is expanding options for design engineers so they can move control functions closer to the processes they support and facilitate flexible deployment outside traditional enclosures. As these systems become more distributed, diagnostic visibility becomes increasingly important. Maintenance teams need to identify the source of a fault without tracing connections through a central control cabinet, helping limit downtime and simplify service procedures.

While distributed architecture implies a distributed I/O system first, which then connects to a central programmable logic controller (PLC), it is possible to expand that definition to also move the control to individual stations, mounted directly on the machines or situated close by. Doing so further simplifies expansion and makes reconfiguration of component modules much easier. These advantages are particularly relevant to flexible manufacturing, where equipment modules, sensors, inspection stations, and production capacity may change over the machine lifecycle. Modular architecture can reduce the scope of some upgrades and repairs, although isolating one module without stopping the line depends on the process and safety design.

Bringing Automation Directly to the Machine

A modular approach also creates opportunities to integrate standard I/O, safety, and motor-control functions into the same distributed architecture. As production requirements change, engineers can add or reconfigure individual modules without redesigning the larger automation system. Supporting this architecture requires hardware that brings operational functions closer to the equipment while allowing the system to expand as manufacturing needs change.

The SIMATIC ET 200pro from Siemens enables engineers to create an entire machine-level automation system by picking from a portfolio of modular components, including digital and analog I/O, motor starters, frequency converters, power modules, and distributed central processing units (CPUs) for integrated machine architectures. When correctly assembled, the SIMATIC ET 200pro system provides an IP65/66/67-rated design and the system can be installed directly at the machine without requiring the protection of a traditional control cabinet.

The system’s distributed I/O products, including modular I/O, safety-related components, motor control solutions, communication modules, and associated connectivity elements, align with cabinet-free automation requirements. Control can be provided through an interface module connected to a higher-level controller or through a distributed CPU that places control directly at the machine. An active backplane supports modular expansion and module replacement during operation, while tool-free connections and simplified mounting and wiring approaches help in the fast setup of modular components.

The portfolio extends distributed automation beyond standard I/O PROFIsafe-compatible modules functional support safety applications, while integrated motor starters and frequency converters add motor-control capabilities. Additionally, communication and interface options support technologies such as RFID and IO-Link, allowing additional field devices to be integrated into the same machine-level architecture. Figure 1 illustrates how these functions fit within the modular ET 200pro architecture.

Figure 1: The modular SIMATIC ET 200pro architecture combines I/O, failsafe modules, motor control, and specialized functions such as RFID and IO-Link within a machine-level automation system. (Source: Siemens)

The Siemens SIMATIC ET 200pro system also supports replacement of electronic modules without disconnecting field wiring, facilitating fast fault tracing and diagnostics. Modules can be hot-swapped while the controller remains in RUN mode, allowing affected electronics to be replaced without stopping the controller or dismantling the surrounding field wiring. This capability helps maintenance teams isolate and address problems at the machine level while minimizing disruption to the automation system.

With IP65/67 ratings for protection against dust and water ingress, the ET 200pro is designed for demanding machine-level environments where cabinet-free installation may be desirable.

Future expansion plans and the related growth of I/O points will help determine whether a distributed architecture is the right fit for an application. Regardless of the architecture selected, grounding, electromagnetic noise mitigation, and signal separation remain important design considerations. Environmental protection requirements, diagnostic visibility, maintenance efficiency, and ease of fault isolation are all factors that can make systems such as the SIMATIC ET 200pro well suited for modern, highly modular automation environments.

Conclusion

As manufacturing adopts increasingly flexible and modular production models, automation platforms must be scalable, rugged, and designed for efficient diagnostics, maintenance, and expansion.

Distributed architectures, whether limited to decentralized I/O placement or transferring control to individual machines, help address the wiring, scalability, and modularity challenges associated with modern automation systems. However, moving I/O and control functions beyond the control cabinet requires careful consideration of environmental protection, diagnostic visibility, maintenance efficiency, and standardization. Solutions such as the SIMATIC ET 200pro illustrate how these requirements can be addressed in machine-level automation systems. By balancing these considerations, engineers can create automation systems that are easier to maintain, expand, and adapt to changing manufacturing requirements.

Author

Poornima Apte is an engineer turned writer with B2B specialties in robotics, AI, cybersecurity, smart technologies and digital transformation. Find her on Twitter @booksnfreshair.

item.title: How Scientific Research Benefits from Modern AI
item.description:
Source: Deemerwha studio/stock.adobe.com

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the pace and scope of scientific discovery in medicine, environmental science, and physics, often by making stages in the research pipeline faster or by altering them with new processes that require significantly less time. Much of that shift relates to a new generation of AI architectures that changed how models learn from data and the depth of representations they can capture. As a result, the progression from hypothesis to results is much faster, making failed attempts less costly in fields where success is rare, such as drug discovery.

This blog explores how modern AI architectures are compressing research timelines across multiple scientific disciplines, where these advances are delivering measurable results today, and the challenges that must be addressed before they can be applied more broadly.

What Changed in Scientific AI

Older statistical machine learning (ML) in science depended on hand-built features. For example, chemists had to decide which molecular descriptors were important for drug design. However, deep learning models, such as transformer and graph-based architectures, instead learn directly from raw sequences, images, or structured graphs. This shift is significant because for many scientific problems, the limiting factor was knowing which features to encode manually. Learning from raw data also enables automated analysis of unstructured inputs like images, allowing experts to process volumes of data that would otherwise be impractical to handle manually. Protein folding is a clear example of a problem that challenged researchers for decades before AI models demonstrated that protein structures could be predicted directly from amino acid sequences.

Medicine: From Protein Structure to Candidate Molecule

AlphaFold2's performance at the 14th Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction (CASP14) contest demonstrated protein structures at an accuracy rivaling experimental methods. Its database now covers over 214 million predicted structures, up from roughly 300,000 when it launched, and has been used by more than 3 million researchers across more than 190 countries.[1] That widespread availability fed directly into drug design. The preclinical phase—from target identification to drug candidate nomination—traditionally takes three to six years. However, AI-native firms like Insilico Medicine completed theirs in under 18 months and reached Phase I clinical trials within 30 months of program initiation.[2] Even though it's not guaranteed that AI-assisted drugs will receive FDA approval, the reduction in both time to trial and costs means pharmaceutical companies have a greater chance of success than ever before.

A similar case shows up in genomics. Missense variants are mutations that alter a single amino acid in a protein and may affect its function. Before the deep learning model AlphaMissense was developed, only about 2 percent of the roughly 4 million such variants in the human genome had been clinically classified.[3] Interpreting the rest required slow, case-by-case laboratory experiments, many of which were left unresolved. AlphaMissense predicts a pathogenicity score for each variant in seconds, though clinical classification still requires confirmation. Digital pathology follows the same pattern. Large deep learning models were trained on over a billion small, standardized image patches extracted from digitized tissue slides. Now, those models can detect rare cancers directly from a scanned biopsy sample.[4] This diagnostic ability previously required hours of manual review by specialist pathologists, an expertise that many hospitals lack.

Environmental Science: Faster Weather Forecasting

In environmental science, AI-based weather models have improved the speed of discovery and the application of results. Traditional weather forecasting divides the atmosphere into a 3D grid of boxes, then uses supercomputers to solve physics equations forward in time, step by step. Where the grid is too coarse to compute directly, simplified representations of small-scale processes like cloud formation are used instead. Models such as GraphCast, however, learn from decades of historical atmospheric data to predict how weather patterns evolve, picking up the real statistical behavior of those small-scale processes instead of relying on simplified formulas.[5]

Because GraphCast skips solving the full physics equations at runtime, it produces a forecast in under a minute on a single chip, compared to hours on a supercomputer, with accuracy that matches or beats traditional systems on most measures. This lets researchers run far more forecasts and scenarios in the same amount of time and at the same cost, accelerating the pace of follow-on research. These models inherit known precipitation biases from their training data, a limitation stemming from their reliance on historical patterns rather than physical laws. Even so, the speed and accuracy gains represent a substantial shift in what is computationally feasible for atmospheric science.

Physics: Predicting Crystal Stability

In materials science, testing a candidate crystal’s stability has meant either synthesizing it in a lab or running quantum-mechanics-based density functional theory (DFT) calculations, both of which are slow and expensive enough to make exhaustive searches of the possible materials space impractical. DeepMind’s Graph Networks for Materials Exploration (GNoME) model predicts a candidate’s stability almost instantly, sends only the most promising ones to DFT for verification, and feeds those results back into the model. This active learning loop boosted the accuracy of stability predictions from around 50 percent to 80 percent on the field’s benchmark.[6] This approach accelerates research because low-cost computational screening combined with selective DFT checks allows GNoME to cover far more of the space of possible materials than DFT alone could. The result was 2.2 million candidate crystals identified, of which 381,000 were confirmed stable, delivered as a pre-filtered shortlist rather than requiring researchers to test candidates one by one.

The Catch: Reproducibility and Opacity

Beyond the data bias and absence of guaranteed results already discussed, a lack of explainability and reproducibility can undermine the reliable use of AI in scientific research. In most cases, these models do not reveal how they arrived at a prediction, which is a more significant limitation in science than in many other uses of machine learning, since scientific outputs must typically support a testable hypothesis. The field of interpretability addresses this by developing methods to examine how input data leads to specific predictions in a measurable way. Reproducing a result also requires access to the same code, parameters, training data, and often comparable computing resources. When these are not shared openly, even non-proprietary results are difficult for others to verify or build on, reducing confidence in the findings and slowing broader adoption.

Conclusion

A common pattern is emerging across medicine, environmental science, and physics. Tasks that once took years, or had no practical solution at all, can now be completed in days, hours, or even minutes, shortening the surrounding research pipeline in the process. Protein structures can be predicted in minutes, variant pathogenicity can be assessed in seconds rather than remaining unresolved indefinitely, and millions of candidate materials can be identified without exhaustive laboratory testing.

What these examples demonstrate is that the acceleration is already measurable, even though the end goal in each field, such as an approved drug or a synthesizable material, has not yet been fully realized. Significant challenges still remain, particularly in interpretability and reproducibility. Addressing these challenges will enable faster research to produce results that are trusted, verified, and ready for wider use cases.

[2] https://insilico.com/phase1
[3] https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00668-9
[4] https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03141-0
[5] https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adi2336
[6] https://deepmind.google/blog/millions-of-new-materials-discovered-with-deep-learning/

item.title: New Tech Tuesdays: Engineering Reliability into Commercial Drones
item.description:
New Tech Tuesdays

Join Mouser's Technical Content team for a weekly look at all things interesting, new, and noteworthy for design engineers.

Remote-controlled (RC) aircraft once meant foam wings, bulky transmitters, and a flight that had a high probability of ending in a tree. Today’s commercial drones—the descendants of those RC aircraft—are much more advanced, offering capabilities such as spreading fertilizer, capturing digital imagery, and transporting packages, among other things. Yet, while the aircraft may be more capable, every additional feature competes for the same limited battery capacity, weight allowance, and space.

Successful commercial drone design requires more than selecting an efficient motor or low-power sensor. This week’s New Tech Tuesdays examines how coordinated power management, propulsion control, and magnetic sensing can support reliable flight, protect critical circuitry, and preserve the energy available for its application-specific functions.

Commercial Drone Design Starts with the Propulsion Chain

A drone’s propeller motors produce the thrust required for vertical lift, directional movement, and attitude control. Each propulsion channel typically combines power conversion, a motor driver, current sensing, and closed-loop motor control. If these elements do not operate together effectively, the result can be wasteful operation, unstable movement, or inadequate protection against electrical faults.

Motor current provides useful feedback because it corresponds to the torque the motor produces. By monitoring current near the motor, the control system gains visibility into changing propulsion loads and can detect overcurrent conditions caused by overloads, short circuits, or other faults.[1] Magnetic current sensors perform this measurement without requiring direct electrical contact between the current-carrying conductor and the sensing circuitry. Depending on the implementation, they can also provide galvanic isolation between the power conductor path and measurement circuitry.

Sensor size and conductor resistance also matter. A compact sensor can fit close to the motor-drive circuitry, while low resistance helps limit conduction losses and heat generation. These characteristics are particularly important in multirotor aircraft because the circuitry is repeated across several propulsion channels.

Flight Time Is a System-Level Challenge

When a drone needs more time in the air, attention typically turns to the battery. Battery capacity is important, but adding a larger battery increases mass, which can require additional thrust and larger propellers, and can consume some of the energy the larger battery was intended to provide.

A more complete approach evaluates losses throughout the power chain. Battery monitoring, direct current-to-direct current (DC/DC) conversion, motor-current sensing, gate driving, lighting, and position sensing all contribute to the total energy budget. Reducing consumption and conduction losses at multiple points may be more practical than relying on a single component change to extend flight time automatically.

Power monitoring also gives the control system better visibility into the battery’s operating state, while efficient voltage regulation supplies lower-voltage electronics without unnecessarily consuming energy reserved for propulsion. The objective is not simply to minimize the power used by each component, but to coordinate the entire chain so that sensing, protection, and control do not impose excessive losses.

Magnetic Sensing Beyond the Propellers

Propulsion may keep a drone airborne, but position sensing helps many of its other functions operate predictably. A camera gimbal, for example, needs to measure angular position so its motors can compensate for aircraft movement and maintain a stable field of view (FOV). Magnetic position sensors can provide contactless angular feedback in compact mechanical assemblies, including configurations that measure movement along one, two, or three axes.[2]

Similar sensing principles apply to handheld controllers. Joysticks, buttons, and triggers experience repeated movement throughout their operating lives. Replacing mechanically contacting position elements with magnetic sensing can reduce wear while maintaining consistent position feedback. Low-power operating modes can further limit controller battery consumption when an input is inactive.

Sensor selection still requires attention to magnetic range, accuracy, linearity, bandwidth, mechanical alignment, and nearby magnetic fields. Contactless operation removes a mechanical wear point, but it does not remove the need for careful design. Physics is still physics.

The Newest Products for Your Newest Designs®

The Allegro MicroSystems robotics portfolio includes solutions for power management, propulsion, and position sensing in commercial drones. The portfolio includes the ACS37800 power-monitoring integrated circuit, A8586 buck converter, ACS71240 current sensor, and A4919 three-phase brushless direct current gate driver for the power and propulsion chain.

For position feedback, the CT8150, CT310, and A31301 magnetic sensors support functions such as gimbal-angle measurement. Additionally, the A1391, A1392, A1393, and A1395 linear sensors can provide sensing for joysticks, buttons, and triggers. Together, these devices enable engineers to address battery monitoring, voltage regulation, motor control, current measurement, camera stabilization, and pilot interfaces as related parts of the drone architecture rather than isolated functions.

Tuesday’s Takeaway

Reliable commercial drones depend on coordinated power management, propulsion, and sensing. To meet these demands, current feedback helps control and protect propeller motors, power-chain optimization makes better use of stored energy, and magnetic position sensing supports stable camera operation and durable pilot-controller interfaces. Evaluating these functions at the system level helps engineers manage trade-offs among flight time, size, weight, protection, and reliability across the aircraft.
