item.title: Ground Fault Protection in Commercial Environments
item.description:
Source: Ekaterina/stock.adobe.com

Electrical equipment is commonly used in a variety of applications where systems and components may be exposed to water. Water increases the risk of electric shock or ground faults by lowering electrical resistance and creating conductive paths for current flow. It can also provide a path for electricity to reach personnel or equipment. Implementing ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection is an effective way to reduce electric-shock risk by disconnecting a circuit when leakage current exceeds the device’s specified trip characteristic.

This blog explores how GFCIs detect and interrupt ground faults and examines common applications where ground-fault protection is essential for safety and compliance.

GFCI Definition and Standards

A GFCI is a device that monitors the outgoing and returning current in a circuit. A differential current transformer within the GFCI measures the difference between the two currents. Current that fails to return to the transformer has found another path to the ground, creating a shock hazard. The GFCI disconnects the circuit if the difference between the outgoing and returning current exceeds the trip threshold, which is 4mA to 6mA in residential circuits. This response occurs within fractions of a second, helping protect individuals from electrical shock if they come into contact with the current.

In contrast, standard circuit breakers are designed to protect equipment from overloads and short circuits. However, they typically cannot detect smaller current differentials that can result in shocks or fires in and around water-adjacent applications. There are several standards engineers should be aware of when implementing GFCIs:

UL Standards

  • UL 943 defines minimum safety standards for GFCI design and functionality, including interrupting the circuit when the ground-fault current falls within the specified Class A operating range, conventionally greater than 4mA and not greater than 6mA. It also requires reverse line-load miswire protection and auto-monitoring functionality to regularly self-check performance.[1]
  • UL 1998 defines a set of safety standards for programmable software with an emphasis on risk analysis and fault detection. UL 1998 requirements are intended to prevent conversion faults between software and hardware, coding faults, timing faults, memory faults, and microelectronic hardware failures.[2]

National Electrical Code (NEC®) Standards

  • NEC 680.5 requires Class A GFCI protection for receptacles and outlets covered by Article 680 on branch circuits rated 150V or less to ground and 60A or less. Class A GFCI devices trip when a ground-fault current of around 4mA to 6mA is detected. It also mandates special-purpose GFCI (SPGFCI) protection, where specified by Article 680, for single-phase and three-phase receptacles and outlets supplied by branch circuits exceeding 150V to ground and not exceeding 480V phase-to-phase. The SPGFCI protection must have a ground-fault trip level that does not exceed 20mA. This code section typically applies to pools, spas, fountains, and similar installations.[3]
  • NEC 210.8A requires GFCI protection for all 125V to 250V receptacles in indoor and outdoor spaces, regardless of the receptacle’s proximity to water. This regulation applies to equipment in residential settings (i.e., dwelling units), including kitchens, basements, and laundry rooms.[4]
  • NEC 210.8B extends the same protections as NEC 210.8A for workplaces (i.e., non-dwelling units).
  • NEC 210.8D requires general GFCI protection for specific appliances (e.g., dishwashers, pressure washers, sump pumps).

Users can trust that UL- and NEC-compliant GFCIs are designed with safety in mind. Safety considerations are especially important in commercial areas.

GFCI Applications

Many workplace environments have elevated risks of electric shock and fire due to their proximity to water.

Commercial Kitchens

The combination of running water, wet surfaces, stainless-steel equipment, and conductive surfaces creates an environment where electrical shock hazards are a significant concern. Many commercial kitchen appliances, including ranges, fryers, and mixers, must be movable to meet sanitation requirements, necessitating that appliances be connected via plugs and flexible cords and cables. Repeated movement, cleaning, and daily operation can cause cords and cables to wear over time, increasing the likelihood of insulation damage and ground faults. Because of the elevated risks in commercial kitchens, NEC 210.8(B) broadly requires GFCI protection for commercial kitchen receptacles running on single-phase circuits up to 50A and three-phase circuits up to 100A, and NEC 210.8(D) identifies specific appliances that always require GFCI protection, such as dishwashers and microwave ovens.

Food and Beverage Processing Facilities

Food and beverage processing facilities undergo frequent washdowns and strict sanitation procedures that expose electrical equipment to moisture, humidity, and other high-moisture conditions. These environments increase the risk of ground faults caused by damaged wiring, cordsets, plugs, and electrical connections. Because personnel routinely operate electrically powered equipment in wet processing areas, the National Electrical Code (NEC) 210.8(B) requires GFCI protection for many receptacles and electrical devices commonly used in these facilities.

Pools, Spas, Fountains, and Water Features

Pumps, heating, lighting, and filtration systems mainly operate near water. To help address the potential electrical hazards, NEC 680.5 commonly applies to equipment implemented in pools, spas, fountains, and other related equipment. Pool pump motors in commercial environments often exceed the 150V-to-ground limit for Class A GFCI devices, so the code calls for SPGFCI protection for circuits above 150V-to-ground up to 480V phase-to-phase.

Vehicle Service and Maintenance Centers

Portable, plug-in equipment is commonly used in automotive service and repair facilities. Welding torches, grinders, metal cutters, and drills all fall into this category. The risk of frayed cables, cords, and wires around water increases the likelihood of shock or fire. Large and hand-held vacuum cleaners, spray washers, and tire-inflation pumps require GFCI protection according to NEC 210.8B. Safety requirements are also rigorously applied to prevent workplace accidents and injuries. Wet floors and automobiles made from highly conductive materials increase those risks.

Although different environments where electricity and water often mix present a variety of challenges, the need for fast and reliable protection from electrical shocks or faults is common to all of the categories.

Ground Fault Protection for Commercial and Industrial Systems

The Littelfuse SB4000 Industrial Shock Block is a versatile GFCI solution designed to meet the needs of a variety of water-adjacent applications. Supporting single-phase, split-phase, three-phase, and 4-wire systems, it is rated for 208V to 240V systems up to 30A and can be used in both solidly grounded and high-resistance grounded systems. The unit provides grounded-neutral protection and a fixed 6mA trip threshold in accordance with UL 943 requirements. Harmonic filtering, automatic self-testing, and UL 1998-compliant software help ensure reliable performance and continuous fault monitoring.

Built for demanding environments, the SB4000 features an IP69K and NEMA 4X-rated polycarbonate enclosure, conformal-coated circuit boards for corrosion resistance, and a 10,000A short-circuit current rating. Together, these features help ensure dependable performance in demanding indoor and outdoor commercial and industrial environments.

Conclusion

Ground fault protection is essential for the safety of personnel and equipment when electrical systems operate near water. Detecting conditions that could result in current leakage, electrical shock, or fire is critical to maintaining safe operation. GFCIs are also necessary to comply with a range of codes and standards that apply to water-adjacent systems and applications. Utilizing a GFCI, such as the SB4000 Shock Block, can provide a safer environment for personnel, maintain equipment integrity, and support regulatory compliance.

item.title: Agentic AI for Industrial Energy Optimization
item.description:
AI agents coordinate energy decisions while meeting production and equipment requirements

Jiraporn/stock.adobe.com; generated with AI

Energy use in industrial equipment is interconnected. For example, reducing consumption in one part of a plant can affect operating conditions or production elsewhere. However, simply seeing a lower reading on an energy-consumption meter does not indicate whether the reduction is workable.

To assess a proposed change, engineers need to know current machine states, production schedules, and equipment operating limits. This information is stored in different systems and often changes during a shift. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents help bring this context together and assess the available options.

In the second part of our blog series on agentic AI’s role in industrial automation, we discussed the ways AI enables predictive maintenance in industrial equipment. In this final blog of the series, we define energy optimization, examine how AI agents could improve energy use and efficiency, and explore how an implementation could work in an industrial automation setting.

Understanding Industrial Energy Optimization

Industrial energy optimization is the practice of choosing how and when equipment operates to improve a defined energy outcome. A facility that aims to reduce electricity consumption, energy cost, peak demand, or emissions associated with its energy use still needs to meet production deadlines, maintain product quality, and stay within equipment and safety limits.

The target measurement will depend on the exact goal. For example, measuring kilowatt-hours per acceptable unit produced shows energy use relative to the output. Another key measurement involves identifying energy cost per production batch, which captures the effect of electricity rates on a particular cycle. Moreover, peak demand measures the highest power draw over a specific interval and idle consumption shows how much energy equipment uses when it is not producing any output.

These measures are not interchangeable. Moving a batch production to a lower-priced period reduces its cost without reducing the energy it consumes. But by prioritizing a lower peak in demand, total consumption remains unchanged. So comparing energy per unit also requires comparable production conditions; otherwise, a change in output could be mistaken for an efficiency gain.

Energy-monitoring systems record these values and alert human operators about the changes. But optimization goes further, using measurements, production schedules, and equipment constraints to compare operating methods for the plant. For instance, high idle consumption points to an opportunity, but shutting down the equipment helps only if the next operation can still start on time.

Using Agentic AI to Support Energy-Efficient Operations

An AI agent brings together energy-monitoring data from separate systems. The agent can call a forecasting model to estimate upcoming demand and an optimization model to compare possible operating plans. The forecast predicts what may happen, while the optimizer evaluates options, such as which approved equipment combination should run. The agent coordinates among different tools and incorporates the results into a recommendation.

The ability to revise a plan becomes important when the operating conditions change frequently. For example, a fixed energy-saving rule follows its predefined response, but a delayed batch makes the response unsuitable. The agent has to retrieve the new schedule, request a forecast, compare the available options, and update its recommendation. Plant personnel would still need to approve consequential changes, showing the necessity for a human-in-the-loop workflow.

Implementing Agentic AI for Industrial Energy Management

As an example implementation, consider an industrial plant with several production lines and shared compressors and chillers. The plant must meet its production target and keep the facility’s demand below a defined limit.

Smart meters and equipment controllers send time-stamped energy measurements and machine states to an industrial data platform. The production system gives the current schedule and output figures.

The AI agent receives the production target and energy objective. It gathers the current operating data and calls forecasting software to estimate the facility’s load over the next several hours.

If the forecasting model indicates a potential demand peak, the AI agent calls an optimization model to identify possible changes. These include changing a process within its completion window, reducing an idle period, or staggering the startup of high-load equipment.

The agent checks for proposed changes to the production schedule and equipment constraints. If the production order changes, the agent must update the analysis or refer the proposal to a human operator.

The implementation should begin in advisory mode, where the agent provides the expected energy effect, the affected equipment, and the constraints. The operator reviews and approves any specific changes. Then, confirmed schedules are applied through the existing manufacturing execution system (MES).

After the recommendations and verification process has proven reliable, the plant operator should consider allowing the agent to automatically submit narrowly defined, reversible actions within approved limits.

Balancing Energy Goals with Operational Constraints

Agentic AI is not designed to magically remove constraints on industrial energy decisions. Many aspects, such as production targets and equipment limits, will continue to determine possible changes. An agent helps integrate current plant data with forecasting and optimization models to identify feasible options.

The significance of using agents lies in coordinating the response, which includes preparing a recommendation, routing approved changes, and verifying that energy performance has improved without disrupting production. However, throughout the process, operators should retain authority over plant operation.

item.title: How Connectivity Enables Humanoid Robotics
item.description:
Source: DangThi/stock.adobe.com

Robots have become common tools across a wide range of applications, each designed to serve a specific purpose. While humanoid robots are unlikely to be mistaken for humans, they are designed to operate in environments built for people, requiring them to navigate spaces, manipulate objects, and perform tasks that are not always optimized for automation. To accomplish this, they integrate machine vision, sensing, artificial intelligence (AI), and precise motion control to interact safely and effectively with the world around them.

Bringing these capabilities together requires the integration of multiple technologies into a single moving machine. From high-speed sensor data and compute systems to motor drives and power distribution networks, each subsystem places different demands on the connectors and cables that support it. Designers must balance electrical performance with the space constraints and mechanical demands of a robot that must maintain reliable operation while in motion.

This blog examines how interconnects support the flow of data, signals, and power between the sensors, compute systems, motors, and power distribution networks that enable humanoid robots to operate in environments designed for people.

Perception

To navigate and interact safely with their surroundings, humanoid robots need to accurately perceive and interpret their environment. Cameras provide the visual information needed for navigation and object recognition, while proximity, force, torque, and other sensors help the robot build a detailed understanding of operating conditions and interactions with nearby objects.

The data generated by these systems places significant demands on the interconnects linking sensors to processing hardware. High-resolution machine-vision systems, in particular, can generate large volumes of data, making the interface essential to overall system performance. Connector selection is often influenced by the machine-vision protocol in use. For example, USB3 Vision is based on USB 3.x, while GigE Vision uses Ethernet connectivity. CoaXPress transmits high-speed image data over coaxial cable. Camera Link and Camera Link HS provide interfaces designed specifically for high-performance imaging applications, with copper and optical connectivity options.[1] Other imaging systems may use Mobile Industry Processor Interface (MIPI) CSI-2 interfaces with flexible flat cables (FFC). Compact FFC/ flexible printed circuit (FPC) connectors are suitable for confined spaces such as a robot's head or torso. Some connectors feature a one-touch locking mechanism that provides secure cable retention.

Working in conjunction with the cameras, proximity, force, and torque sensors allow the robot to detect and measure its interactions with surrounding objects. Depending on the device, sensor outputs may be digital or analog and can have very different bandwidth requirements. As a result, connector selection should be based on each sensor's specific requirements rather than treating perception as a single network.

Once collected, this sensor and imaging data must be transmitted to the robot's compute systems and processed with minimal delay so the robot can respond effectively to changes in its environment.

Compute

Processing sensor and imaging data with minimal latency is essential for humanoid robots that operate alongside humans. Transmitting large volumes of data to remote computing resources can introduce delays and make operation dependent on external networks. Edge computing helps address these challenges by enabling time-critical decisions to be made using onboard processing hardware.

Supporting these internal data flows places significant demands on the robot’s connectivity infrastructure. As data rates increase, maintaining signal integrity becomes more challenging because connectors, PCB traces, and cable assemblies are all part of the signal path and collectively affect the performance of the entire channel.

These requirements are further complicated by the human-like form factors of humanoid robots. Unlike conventional industrial computers, components must fit within a compact, human-shaped structure that leaves little room for bulky connectors. Designers cannot simply increase the enclosure size to simplify packaging, and every additional component adds mass that the robot's actuators must move.

High-density connectors help support high data rates within the limited space available for the compute systems. Consequently, connector selection becomes a careful balance between electrical performance, mechanical packaging, and overall system design.

Actuation

Humanoid robots must translate computational decisions into physical motion. Electric motors throughout the robot drive joints and other mechanisms, forming a complex control system that continuously responds to sensor inputs.

Motor drivers and controllers provide the interface between the robot's computing system and its motors, which means they require connections for both control and power. Communication technologies such as SPI, EtherCAT, or RS-485 carry commands from the compute system, while separate power connections then deliver the energy required to drive the motors.

Controlling a humanoid joint involves more than simply commanding a motor to move. Motion occurs within a continuous feedback loop in which sensors monitor motor position, speed, and load, enabling the controller to compare expected and actual movement and make real-time adjustments.

To balance, manipulate objects, and navigate uneven terrain, humanoid robots must coordinate movements across multiple joints simultaneously. These tasks depend on reliable data transfer to support rapid feedback and precise motion control.

A single actuator assembly may require multiple connections for control signals, sensor feedback, and power within a limited space. Because connectors are often located near moving joints, they need to maintain reliable electrical and mechanical performance despite repeated motion and vibration. These demanding operating conditions require interconnect solutions that preserve signal integrity and electrical continuity while delivering long-term mechanical reliability throughout the robot's motion-control system.

Power

Power is distributed through the battery management system to the robot's compute, sensing, and motion-control subsystems. These connections must deliver the required current while minimizing resistance and heat generation. Because the motors that enable complex humanoid motion can place substantial demands on the power system, efficient power distribution is essential for maximizing operating time.

Power connectors must remain securely mated even under repeated movement and vibration, which place mechanical stress on cables and connectors. Increased contact resistance in high-current connections can generate excess heat and increase the risk of arcing. As a result, positive locking mechanisms are especially valuable in mobile robotic systems. Connectors such as Molex MiniCirc Circular Connectors combine a compact circular design with vibration resistance and provide tactile feedback when fully mated.

Humanoid Connectivity Solutions

From sensor networks to power delivery systems, no single interconnect architecture is optimal for every robotic system. Humanoid robots place diverse demands on their interconnect infrastructure, highlighting the need for application-specific connectivity solutions. Perception and compute systems require compact, high-speed data connections, while actuation systems combine control, feedback, and power delivery within tightly constrained spaces. Power distribution systems place additional emphasis on current-carrying capacity, connector retention, and mechanical durability. Meeting these varied requirements requires designers to balance electrical performance, mechanical reliability, and packaging constraints across the robot.

Drawing on decades of experience in automotive and industrial applications, Molex offers connectivity solutions designed to meet the challenges of humanoid robotics, including SlimStack connectors for compact perception systems, Mirror Mezz backplane connectors for high-speed compute, and physically secure Micro-Lock Plus connectors for actuators.[2] Rather than relying on a single connectivity approach throughout the robot, designers can select interconnects tailored to the electrical, mechanical, and packaging requirements of each subsystem. This approach supports the reliable transfer of data, signals, and power throughout the robot.

Conclusion

Humanoid robots combine perception, compute, actuation, and power systems within a single moving platform. Reliable operation depends on interconnects that can support diverse signal, data, and power requirements while withstanding the space constraints and mechanical stresses inherent to humanoid robot designs. By matching connector and cable-assembly solutions to the specific needs of each subsystem, designers can help ensure reliable communication, control, and power delivery throughout the robot. As humanoid robots become more capable, interconnect selection will remain a foundational design consideration affecting performance, reliability and maintainability.

Author

David Pike is well known across the interconnect industry for his passion and general geekiness. His online name is Connector Geek.

item.title: Exploring the Electronics Aboard AC75 and AC40 Foiling Yachts
item.description:
Source: ©Nicolas Touze/La Roche-Posay Racing Team

Modern America’s Cup racing yachts are high-speed embedded systems platforms that use onboard sensors, telemetry, control loops, power conversion, and cockpit interfaces to help crews manage stability, drag, hydraulic response, and foil position. The competition features two classes of foiling yachts: the 12-metre AC40, used for preliminary regattas and the Women’s and Youth America’s Cup, and the 23-metre AC75, the team-specific design that contests the match.[1]

Mouser has joined La Roche-Posay Racing Team as an Official Supporter for the team’s campaign in the 38th Louis Vuitton America’s Cup. The partnership gives the French challenger access to performance-critical electronic components, supporting the onboard systems that keep the team’s foiling race yachts stable, fast, and reliable.

This blog looks at why electronics have become central to America’s Cup performance, how the team’s AC75 boat copes with the demands of the marine environment, and what component availability and traceability mean for a campaign built on rapid, data-driven improvement.

Why Electronics Are Central to America’s Cup Performance

Modern America’s Cup boats are tightly integrated, embedded platforms whose electronics—including telemetry, sensor fusion, and networked electronics architectures—support performance, control, monitoring, and safety-related functions. Mark Patrick, Technical Content Director at Mouser EMEA, describes today’s AC75s as “effectively flying embedded systems platforms,” where the deciding factor is how quickly a team can turn that data into performance improvements. For the 2027 AC75, batteries replace the cyclor teams—crew members pedaling stationary bikes—that previously supplied hydraulic power. A new onboard data crew member monitors how the limited stored energy is allocated among trimming, mast rotation, and foil-cant functions, making power monitoring and control part of the race strategy. Engineers analyse the data both during and after testing sessions to refine foil positioning, hydraulic response, and energy management, continuously updating the digital models that guide development.

That speed of iteration puts real pressure on component reliability, system integration, and supply chain support. For critical systems, such as flight control, power conversion, and telemetry, teams typically apply dual sourcing to ensure supply continuity, along with full component traceability and life cycle monitoring to safeguard design decisions. Quality controls, including moisture-sensitive device (MSD) protection, electrostatic discharge (ESD)-safe storage and assembly practices, and authenticity verification, help ensure components perform reliably under extreme load.

Engineering for the Marine Environment

Onboard electronics and interconnect systems must perform under conditions few embedded systems ever face: constant vibration, moisture exposure, saltwater, and electromagnetic interference (EMI)—all at racing speed. That places significant demands on component quality, system integration, and long-term reliability, since even a small delay in actuator response or control-loop timing can affect drag, stability, and flight behaviour. Reliable electronics integration and deterministic system performance have become genuine competitive advantages, not just engineering requirements.

Powering the AC40 and AC75 Foiling Yachts

In both the AC40 and AC75 classes, real-time data from onboard sensors informs small adjustments, such as foil position or hydraulic response, that balance lift, drag, stability, and maneuverability over the course of a race. That level of responsiveness depends on instrumentation and control systems that continue performing accurately at speed, under load, and in a marine environment. To find out more, explore the Mouser eBook on how electronics are being used on La Roche-Posay Racing Team’s sailboats (Figure 1).

Figure 1: A La Roche-Posay racing yacht on the water. (Source: ©Nicolas Touze/La Roche-Posay Racing Team)

Component Supply as a Performance Driver

Procurement quality, traceability, and handling directly affect the team’s preparation for on-water results. Missing parts limit testing time and compress validation cycles ahead of races, which can carry through to performance on the water. Authorised distribution also plays a role in compliant handling and supply continuity during these compressed cycles: Engineering teams often analyse telemetry immediately after a testing session, implement configuration updates overnight, and validate the changes during the next on-water run (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Pia Mathias, embedded systems engineer, discusses her project with the La Roche-Posay Racing Team. (Source: Mouser)

Looking Ahead to Naples 2027

The 38th Louis Vuitton America’s Cup will be held in Naples in 2027, the first time the event has been staged in Italy. “Performance in today’s America’s Cup is no longer driven by sailing talent alone, but by the ability to integrate cutting-edge technologies into every aspect of the project,” says Stephan Kandler, CEO of La Roche-Posay Racing Team. As the team continues development and testing ahead of the match, its partnership with Mouser is intended to enhance the reliability, precision, and competitiveness of its onboard electronic systems, reinforcing the growing role that component-level engineering plays in elite sailing performance.

item.title: Industrial Ethernet Modernization with PoE Injectors
item.description:
Source: thexfilephoto/stock.adobe.com

Across manufacturing facilities and infrastructure, Ethernet-connected devices have become increasingly common. As networks expand to support more connected equipment, the need to deliver both data and power to distributed endpoints continues to grow. Running separate power and data cables to each device can increase installation time, material cost, routing complexity, and maintenance requirements. Power over Ethernet (PoE) simplifies the connection by delivering power and data over the same Ethernet cable. In existing networks, PoE injectors provide another benefit by enabling PoE functionality without needing to replace non-PoE switches. This blog examines the deployment challenges facing industrial Ethernet networks, as well as the changing connectivity needs in these environments and how PoE injectors can support network modernization.

The Deployment Challenge Behind Industrial PoE

Separating power and data cabling complicates industrial network deployments because each additional cable must be routed, installed, and maintained. This increases installation time and the amount of infrastructure surrounding the connected equipment. As networks expand, those additional runs can add material and deployment costs and make future changes to physical layouts more difficult. Using a single Ethernet cable for both power and data can reduce the cabling burden and simplify connections to distributed devices (Figure 1).

Figure 1: A legacy security camera network requires separate connections for power and data to each camera. (Source: Author)

For existing equipment in these facilities, many industrial networks already rely on Ethernet switches that do not provide PoE. Replacing those switches solely to add power delivery can increase cost and disrupt upgrades. PoE injectors offer an alternative by supplying power to the Ethernet connection between an existing non-PoE switch and a PoE-capable device, enabling designers to add power while continuing to use much of the existing network infrastructure. This solution also gives them more flexibility when equipment is added or relocated.

Modernization is not only about adding connections, though. Industrial networking equipment often operates in environments where extreme heat or cold, moisture, dust, and vibration can affect long-term reliability. PoE connections must maintain reliable power and data transmission under harsh operating conditions, often without active cooling and instead relying on passive heat sinks and rugged enclosures. Features such as surge protection and electrical isolation can help protect equipment from electrical disturbances, while diagnostic functions give maintenance teams greater insight into conditions along the connection.

Why Industrial Networks Are Moving Toward Simplified Edge Connectivity

Diagnostic visibility into network conditions becomes even more important as industrial networks expand and integrate more connected devices. Low latency and dependable connectivity are essential for enabling data filtering and processing at the edge rather than in the cloud. Real-time monitoring and predictive maintenance at the edge are crucial to initiating timely automated responses to potential safety concerns and technical malfunctions.

Networked machines and equipment in manufacturing facilities can exchange sensor and status data across an automated production process in which data collected and analyzed by a sensor on one machine can inform the response of another machine along the production path. Similarly, networked infrastructure such as traffic control systems can use information collected from distributed cameras and sensors to inform decisions elsewhere in the system.

As the networks become more connected, they must also meet higher expectations for uptime and maintainability. Simplifying edge connectivity can make it easier to add or relocate devices while limiting changes to existing infrastructure. PoE injectors are one way to extend edge connectivity without requiring otherwise functional non-PoE switches to be replaced.

Applying PoE Injectors in Existing Industrial Ethernet Networks

By using twisted-pair network cabling, PoE injectors enable data and low-voltage direct current to be delivered simultaneously over a single transmission path. These injectors’ ability to be implemented in conjunction with non-PoE switches helps avoid costly and time-consuming replacement of pre-existing equipment. Single-cable power and data delivery to edge devices in production environments and infrastructure significantly reduces the number of cables and connections required to operate those devices and provides designers with greater flexibility both during the initial design phase and when relocating equipment or integrating additional devices later (Figure 2).

Figure 2: A PoE injector adds power to data from an existing non-PoE Ethernet switch, enabling power and data to be delivered over a single cable to connected devices. (Source: Author)

While simplifying the connection is important in an industrial environment, the equipment must also be protected from electrical conditions that could disrupt communication or damage connected devices.

A key protection feature of PoE injectors is surge protection against transient overvoltage that can result in port failures and device burnout. Surge protection is a critical factor in outdoor applications that may be exposed to lightning or buildings with separate or poor grounding. Another essential form of protection comes from electrical and galvanic isolation that prevents ground loops and low-frequency noise, reducing the potential for damage to connected devices.

Industrial PoE systems can also provide more visibility into potential problems. Shield-current monitoring provides diagnostic data to help identify potential grounding issues during implementation and to support predictive maintenance by revealing conditions that may lead to equipment failures or malfunctions, thereby extending equipment lifetimes and reducing maintenance and costly network downtime.

For industrial and infrastructure applications, Phoenix Contact's PoE injector portfolio delivers power and data over a single cable while incorporating these protection and diagnostic features. The injectors provide integrated surge protection, galvanic isolation, and shield-current monitoring to protect against potential short circuits and shield currents resulting from potential differences between network and device grounds, as well as electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) interference. The Phoenix Contact PoE injectors also support multiple connection technologies for design flexibility and can add PoE capability to Ethernet links from existing non-PoE switches.

Conclusion

Implementing PoE injectors in existing networks can modernize power and data delivery without a complete system overhaul. By reducing the number of cables and field connections required, designers can create simpler installations with greater flexibility for compatible powered devices. Integrated surge protection, electrical isolation, and shield-current indication can improve protection and make certain field-wiring problems easier to identify during commissioning and maintenance. Together, these capabilities provide a practical way to expand industrial networks with additional connected devices while avoiding the cost, complexity, and downtime associated with extensive recabling and system-wide retrofits.

Author

Alex Pluemer is a senior technical writer for Wavefront Marketing specializing in advanced electronics, emerging technologies and responsible technology development.

item.title: New Tech Tuesdays: Giving Voice Interfaces a Better Sense of Direction
item.description:
New Tech Tuesdays

Join Mouser's Technical Content team for a weekly look at all things interesting, new, and noteworthy for design engineers.

Voice interfaces are moving into devices that must hear people from across a room or in spaces where other sounds compete with speech, finding their way into everything from robots and kiosks to collaborative displays, speakerphones, and other interactive devices. Distance can make clear audio difficult to receive. The microphones capture the speaker along with room reflections and background noise. A device with its own loudspeaker also has to contend with acoustic echo.

Recent work with compact microphone arrays shows how much of this processing can now be handled in embedded hardware. Researchers demonstrated a four-microphone system that uses real-time beamforming and direction-of-arrival processing to locate and track a speaker.[1] The system’s combination of fast audio processing and minimal resource use makes it suitable for real-time applications ranging from voice interfaces to videoconferencing and service robots.

This voice processing technology is appearing in newer types of interactive hardware. At CES 2026, the Reachy Mini desktop robot was demonstrated with a ReSpeaker module. The four-microphone system provides far-field voice capture and speaker localization, enabling the robot to determine where a voice is coming from.[2]

In both examples, a combination of directional information from microphone arrays and onboard processing provides clear voice signals.

In this week’s New Tech Tuesdays, we explore how microphone arrays, beamforming, acoustic echo cancellation, and other onboard processing techniques improve far-field voice capture in interactive devices.

From Microphone Array to Usable Speech

Because a microphone array captures the same sound at slightly different times at each microphone, the differences give the processor information about the direction the sound came from. Direction-of-arrival (DoA) processing uses this information to estimate the speaker’s location. Beamforming combines the microphone signals to focus on the direction from which they arrive. Sound arriving from anywhere else can then be reduced relative to the desired speech.

An onboard loudspeaker can introduce another signal that must be removed, since some of the speaker’s sound will feed back into the microphones. Acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) compares the microphone input with a reference of the audio being sent to the loudspeaker, allowing the processor to identify and reduce the loudspeaker audio that comes back through the microphones.[3]

Other processing can clean up the remaining audio interference. Noise suppression reduces unwanted background sound, and automatic gain control adjusts the signal level when a person speaks more quietly or moves further away from the microphone. These combined techniques help produce a cleaner voice signal for speech recognition, communications, or other processing.

The Newest Products for Your Newest Designs®

Handling these audio processing functions in real time requires significant processing at the endpoint. The XMOS VocalFusion® XVF3800 voice processor combines far-field voice processing for four digital microphones in a single device. It provides acoustic echo cancellation, adaptive beamforming, and noise suppression, along with automatic gain control and direction-of-arrival information.

The XVF3800, the voice processor behind the ReSpeaker module used in the Reachy Mini demonstration at CES 2026, uses three beams to locate and follow speakers. One scans for a new speaker, and the other two beams can track individual speakers. It covers 360 degrees and has a specified operating distance of up to 5m. The microphone array can be arranged in either a linear or square configuration.

Tuesday’s Takeaway

Far-field voice depends on more than just detecting speech. A device must also determine where the voice is coming from and separate it from other sounds reaching the microphone. Microphone arrays paired with onboard audio processing enable much of this work to be handled at the endpoint, opening the door to more responsive voice control in robots, kiosks, and other interactive devices.

Automation has transformed agricultural machinery. Modern tractors, sprayers, harvesters, and other farm equipment are no longer merely mechanical equipment. Instead, they function as distributed embedded systems that integrate sensors, cameras, positioning data, electronic controls, actuators, telematics, and artificial intelligence (AI) to monitor conditions, make decisions, and manage resources.

Across many types of agricultural machinery, advanced technologies perform specialized functions. Soil sensors monitor moisture saturation, pH, and nutrient levels, while embedded cameras provide real-time visibility of crop conditions. Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) supply the positioning data that guidance and control systems need for precision spraying, planting, and harvesting. Custom electronic control units (ECUs) embedded in equipment optimize fuel consumption and water distribution via automated irrigation systems, while actuators in harvesters and picking machines enhance efficiency and productivity. Telematics and AI algorithms integrate data from these technologies, analyzing camera and sensor data to improve equipment operation and resource utilization (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Modern agricultural machinery integrates cameras, sensors, antennas, telemetry, displays, controllers, gateways, and network infrastructure throughout the vehicle, creating an increasingly interconnected electronic system. (Source: TE Connectivity, modified by Mouser)

The adoption of these technologies is already widespread. According to the USDA Economic Research Service, 70 percent of large-scale US crop farms in 2023 reported using autosteering guidance systems for machinery, while 68 percent reported using yield monitors and yield or soil mapping technologies.[1] As agricultural equipment becomes more automated and connected, power requirements, data processing demands, and the need for greater interconnectivity increase.

As additional sensors, cameras, and connected systems are integrated into agricultural equipment, designers must ensure that power, data, and control signals move reliably across increasingly complex machines. This article examines the engineering challenges that accompany that complexity and the technologies that help maintain dependable system performance.

Maintaining End-to-End System Reliability

More sensors, cameras, and connected systems in automated agricultural environments increase the potential for technical issues with systems and components. Every new device added to a machine brings more than just another data source. Depending on the system architecture, it may also introduce additional connectors, cabling, network traffic, processing requirements, and power demands. Each of those creates another potential point of failure where power delivery or communication can be disrupted.

As system complexity grows, designers must also address challenges related to signal integrity and electromagnetic interference (EMI), particularly for cameras that generate and transmit large volumes of visual data while sharing network resources with other sensors and control systems. A poor connection, degraded signal, transmission delay, or power interruption anywhere along the data path can affect the flow of information from the sensor to the systems that depend on it. As a result, maintaining reliable operation requires preserving the integrity of the entire system and maintaining processes to continuously monitor its performance.

The operation of an automated precision sprayer illustrates this challenge. The process begins when an embedded camera captures an image depicting the condition of crops. The system transmits the image to an edge processor that analyzes it and determines what action the sprayer should take. A controller issues a command to the sprayer, which is transmitted via the network to begin an operation. An actuator opens the appropriate valve or nozzle, and feedback—such as valve position, flow rate, pressure, or actuator status—verifies that the controller’s command has been executed. A fault in a single component anywhere along the path from edge sensor to performance confirmation can derail the operation. When scaled across a large farm managing fleets of sprayers, tillers, tractors, and other connected equipment, the number of potential failure points increases rapidly. Therefore, ensuring reliable machine operation requires robust interconnects, dependable communication pathways, and continuous monitoring throughout the system.

Designing for Agricultural Operating Conditions

Another major challenge when automating farming processes is the physical environment in which components and equipment must perform. Outdoor farming exposes the physical data path to a variety of potential threats and contaminants that can cause short- and long-term faults and degradation. Dust, mud, and moisture are constantly present in agricultural applications and can potentially damage or erode components, cables, and connectors. Large agricultural machines are susceptible to vibrations from normal operation or from the rugged surroundings they operate in. They are often exposed to chemicals and fertilizers that corrode metals or chemically degrade susceptible cables and surfaces, and typically must be pressure-washed to be thoroughly cleaned. In addition, temperature cycling in motorized equipment creates mechanical strain, and UV exposure can erode cables and components over time.

As a result, equipment and components require strong sealing to prevent the ingress of liquids and particles. Shielding from UV exposure also reduces long-term degradation and increases equipment lifespan, a major factor in reducing overall costs. Cable routing and strain relief are essential for reducing cable exposure to heat, contaminants, and weather, thereby maintaining overall system reliability. It is critical that automated agricultural equipment be robust and reliable enough to meet the spectrum of challenges posed by their physical environments.

Managing Growing Data and Bandwidth Demands

Cameras, sensors, and automation all increase demand for bandwidth as they become more integrated into agricultural machinery and equipment. Modern farming machinery contains embedded cameras that stream data over the network to edge processors or control centers. Machine vision and lidar systems generate large volumes of information that must be transmitted and processed quickly enough to support real-time operational decisions. GNSS positioning accuracy depends on factors such as satellite geometry, signal quality, multipath, atmospheric errors, receiver design, and, in high-precision systems, the availability of correction data such as real-time kinematic (RTK) and precise point positioning (PPP).

Imagery, data collected from soil sensors, and satellite positioning can be used to create prescription maps that help farmers optimize crop production and resource management, thereby further increasing demand for bandwidth. Telematics systems help farmers monitor and coordinate fleets of agricultural equipment in real time, while onboard diagnostics continuously assess equipment health to identify issues before they lead to costly repairs or downtime.

The Agricultural Industry Electronics Foundation (AEF) High-Speed ISOBUS Project conducted simulations of automated farming machines equipped with three to five cameras, operating at speeds ranging from 14Mbps to 75Mbps and delivering packets varying from 42 bytes to 1500 bytes. The simulation indicated that a 100Mbps network could meet immediate and readily forecast needs, although a 1Gbps network may be required for larger-scale and future use cases.[2] As the number of sensors and inputs grows, network speeds will have to increase to meet the greater demand. Large-scale agricultural operations may be operating hundreds of interconnected machines simultaneously, and sufficient bandwidth is necessary to maintain efficient and reliable performance

As of 2026, High-Speed ISOBUS remains under development, with AEF targeting HSI 1.0 for 2028.

Building Robust Agricultural Connectivity Systems

To meet the data transmission and reliability needs of modern precision agriculture, TE Connectivity offers a suite of robust agriculture solutions. TE’s AMPSEAL connectors provide environmental sealing for applications exposed to moisture, dust, and extreme temperatures, and DEUTSCH DT environmentally sealed connectors support wire-to-wire and wire-to-board connections. Single- and multi-port antennas support wireless connectivity across agricultural machinery, while cable assemblies and heat-shrink tubing help protect and maintain connections throughout the physical data path. Together, these technologies provide designers with options for building the robust power, data, and signal paths required by increasingly connected and automated agricultural equipment.

Enabling the Next Generation of Smart Farm Equipment

As agricultural machinery becomes more automated and connected, reliable operation depends on more than rugged equipment. Power, data, and control signals must move dependably across increasingly complex systems while withstanding harsh environmental conditions. Robust interconnect solutions help maintain connectivity, support growing bandwidth demands, and enable reliable performance across modern agricultural equipment.

item.title: New Tech Tuesdays: Scaling High-Voltage Interconnection Systems for EV Architectures
item.description:
New Tech Tuesdays

Join Mouser's Technical Content team for a weekly look at all things interesting, new, and noteworthy for design engineers.

The increasing trend toward vehicle electrification has changed the demands placed on high-voltage interconnects. Beyond carrying substantial current between the battery, inverter, motor, and power-distribution equipment, these systems must fit within limited installation space while controlling electrical losses, heat, and mechanical stress.

In this week’s New Tech Tuesdays, we examine how scalable contact architectures and flexible connector packaging help engineers optimize high‑voltage interconnects for different vehicle platforms, and why electrical, thermal, mechanical, and serviceability requirements must be balanced to achieve reliable EV power distribution.

High-Voltage Interconnection Systems Carry More Than Current

In an electric vehicle (EV) or hybrid electric vehicle (HEV), the high-voltage network connects multiple power-conversion and propulsion subsystems. The US Department of Energy states that vehicle power electronics process and control electrical energy flow, with inverters converting battery-supplied direct current into alternating current for the traction motor.[1]

Every connection along that path contributes some electrical resistance. Since resistive power loss increases with the square of current, even a small connector resistance can become significant as current rises. The resulting heat affects conductor selection, terminal design, surrounding materials, and the thermal margin available under sustained load.

Rated current by itself provides incomplete selection criteria. Engineers need to consider conductor cross-section, ambient temperature, duty cycle, terminal resistance, and the connector’s validated operating conditions. Changes in any of these conditions can affect the connector’s current-carrying capacity and thermal performance.

Matching the EV Connector to the Architecture

A mid-power passenger vehicle and a heavier all-wheel-drive vehicle place distinctly different demands on EV power distribution. Acceleration, towing, hill climbing, and sustained operation under load can require higher current delivery, but selecting the largest available connector for every vehicle may add unnecessary cable mass, packaging volume, integration complexity, and cost.

A tiered high-voltage interconnection system gives engineers another option. An EV/HEV platform can use an interconnect sized for its expected load profile while retaining a related, higher-capacity architecture for more demanding vehicle options. This approach supports design reuse without forcing every model to carry the penalties associated with the highest power tier.

The US Department of Energy identifies reduced weight and volume, improved efficiency and reliability, and modular, scalable design as important objectives for electric-drive systems.[2] Connector selection contributes to each of these factors since the interconnect can influence cable size, routing, thermal performance, assembly space, and mechanical interfaces.

Packaging and Serviceability Join the Circuit

Selecting the conductor size is only one part of high-voltage cable integration. High-voltage cables also require routing clearance, bend space, strain management, shielding continuity, and access for assembly. Connector orientation can determine whether the cable follows a practical path or competes with structural members, coolant lines, and other nearby electronics.

Service access deserves equal attention. Lever-assisted mating, visible assurance features, and configurable cable exits can simplify installation and help technicians verify that a connection is fully seated. For high-voltage equipment, touch protection and environmental sealing are also essential design considerations. International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 60529 defines the IP Code, which classifies enclosure protection against access to hazardous parts, ingress of solid foreign objects, and harmful effects caused by water ingress.[3] By addressing routing, accessibility, and protection early in the design process, engineers can create safer and more serviceable high-voltage systems.

The Newest Products for Your Newest Designs®

TE Connectivity’s HC-STAK 25 XE High-Voltage Interconnection System targets mid-power EV and HEV applications. The system supports up to 1,000VDC and up to 296A continuously at +85°C with a 70mm² conductor. Its layered 2.5mm fork-terminal architecture provides up to 40 contact points per circuit, while optional bidirectional cable routing permits 180° plug rotation. A cam-driven lever and front-facing connector position-assurance feature support installation and service access.

For higher-output and heavier vehicle platforms, the TE Connectivity HC-STAK 35 High-Voltage Interconnection System supports up to 1,000VDC and up to 400A continuously at +85°C with a 95mm² conductor. Its 3.5mm double-ended fork terminals provide up to 64 contact points per circuit. Both systems specify a −40°C to +125°C operating range and incorporate shielded, touch-safe, vibration-resistant construction for demanding vehicle environments.

Tuesday’s Takeaway

Selecting a high-voltage interconnection system is ultimately an exercise in balanced engineering. The best choice provides sufficient current capacity and design margin while controlling resistance, heat, cable mass, packaging demands, and service complexity. Connectors with different current tiers allow engineers to use a common design approach while matching interconnect performance to each vehicle’s specific power requirements.

item.title: Mobile Cobots for Flexible Industrial Automation
item.description:
Mobile cobots combine autonomous transport with robotic handling across industrial workflows

Source: Nay/stock.adobe.com

Industrial manufacturers must constantly adapt to changing production schedules, batch sizes, and labor constraints. These conditions make it harder to justify fixed automation designed for a single product or workstation. Automation must move where work is needed and switch between tasks as demand changes.

For example, mobile collaborative robots (cobots) combine robotic arms that can handle and manipulate parts with autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) that can navigate between locations. This combination gives the cobot a facility-wide working area and enables it to connect production steps that depend on manual transfers.

In this first part of our blog series on cobots in automation, we look at how mobile cobots automate handoffs between operations and which workflows benefit from this mobility. We also examine the engineering work needed to make the complete system reliable.

Automating the Handoffs Between Operations

Combining mobility and part handling is useful for automating handoffs between separate production steps.

For example, consider a mobile cobot tending a computer numerical control (CNC) machine. Production software sends a service request once the machine finishes its cycle, and the cobot collects the correct blank from a staging area.

When the cobot reaches the CNC machine, it must establish the correct working position. The machine controller checks that the spindle has stopped and the door is open before giving access.

The cobot removes the finished part and places it in onboard storage. It loads the new blank and confirms the exchange. The CNC machine can then start its next cycle as the cobot takes the finished part to inspection.

This sequence has to operate as one mission. If a mission has 10 stages and each stage succeeds on 99 percent of attempts, only about 90 percent of missions will complete without any exceptions.

Retries also add time and require clear rules. A mobile cobot’s main value comes from automating these handoffs and ensuring that automation is reliable.

Choosing Workflows That Benefit from Mobility

In effective industrial environments, tasks should be spread across several stations and each should require robotic part handling only at intervals. The cobot must have enough time to travel to the station and complete the exchange before production is delayed.

Total service time includes arm movement, travel, and docking time, while traffic or routine retries add variation. Engineers need to compare the complete service time with the rate at which stations request the cobot.

In the case of several CNC machines sharing one mobile cobot, each time a machine finishes a cycle, it requests a part exchange. The cobot may need about two minutes to travel to the machine, dock, and complete the exchange.

If the requests are spaced apart, the cobot can move from one machine to the next without affecting production. But if two machines request service at the same time, one has to wait while the cobot finishes the first task. Engineers need to make sure these waiting times do not become long enough to delay production.

This timing model helps identify suitable applications. In production flow, a mobile cobot can move works in progress between cells and place them at the next assembly stage. Material supply tasks can include preparing kits or replenishing line-side bins. Beneficial to these scenarios is that the cobot’s arm removes the need for a transfer mechanism at every destination.

Inspection and logistics are also examples where the task moves between locations. The cobot can carry an inspection instrument to a large workpiece, avoiding the need to move the part. In a warehouse, the cobot can transfer totes from storage to packing and bring items from the same order.

Software-based routes make it easier to reassign the platform when products or layouts change. When this occurs, engineers can update the map and task program without installing a new conveyor. However, each new task must be tested because the workstation and operating conditions have changed.

Mobile cobots make sense when the value of sharing a single arm across multiple locations outweighs the time lost to travel and docking.

Considerations for Reliable Deployment

Engineers must address several key factors when designing mobile cobots into an automation environment. AMRs can arrive close enough to identify the correct station yet be too far for the cobot to place a part into a fixture. Most industrial systems solve this in two stages: Navigation brings the platform into the station area, and docking establishes the working frame for the arm.

The final tool position can be affected by errors throughout the entire system. The AMR may not stop at the same point on every visit. Docking has a repeatability limit. Movement in the chassis changes the cobot’s base position, while arm repeatability and fixture position add further error.

Robot repeatability data assume that the arm is attached to a fixed base. It does not include movement from tires, suspension, or docking. Engineers have to work backward from the process tolerance and decide how much error each part of the system might contribute.

Mechanical integration also changes the working limits. The mobile base must be able to support the arm and its controller before any production payload is added. Tooling and onboard storage use more of the available capacity. The remaining payload availability must cover every part carried during the mission.

Battery state affects which missions the cobot accepts. The cobot needs to reserve the battery for picking up the part, completing the delivery, and reaching the charger. Time spent waiting for machines also reduces availability, with traffic holds and docking further reducing it.

Recovery logic is just as important as normal operation. Blocked routes can change arrival time and cause a station reservation to expire. If a workstation becomes unavailable after pickup, the cobot needs a safe place to wait or hold the part. These responses should be defined before deployment because an operator cannot safely improvise every recovery.

Conclusion

Mobile cobots bridge the gap between material transport and robotic handling, enabling a single automation platform to connect multiple production processes. Their strongest use case lies in environments where work is distributed across several stations and automation needs to adapt as production demands change.

However, successful deployment depends on more than combining an AMR with a robotic arm. Engineers must account for travel time, docking accuracy, payload limits, battery management, and recovery logic to ensure reliable operation across the entire workflow. When these factors are addressed, mobile cobots can reduce manual handoffs, improve resource utilization, and provide a flexible alternative to fixed automation infrastructure.

In the next installation of our cobot blog series, we turn our attention toward the advanced vision systems giving cobots enhanced depth perception and more precise object recognition.

item.title: Selecting Anti-Vandal Switches for Industrial Control Panels
item.description:
(Source: Nuttapon/stock.adobe.com)

Push buttons and switches are among the simplest components on an industrial control panel, but they are also among the most exposed. Industrial controls require durable, easy-to-use interfaces between the operator and the panel. These interfaces must withstand repeated actuation and exposure to harsh operating conditions. They are frequently subjected to moisture, liquids, dust, and other particles. Outdoor installations may also encounter temperature extremes, changing weather conditions, and tampering.

Because switches are mounted at the enclosure boundary, they must hold up to both repeated operator use and environmental exposure. Anti-vandal switches are panel-mounted push buttons designed for these demanding conditions, combining metal housings with environmental sealing to provide added protection.

Selecting an anti-vandal switch involves more than choosing a rugged push button. This blog explores how Ingress Protection (IP) ratings, housing construction, actuator style, illumination options, and switch behavior affect switch selection, helping designers match environmental protection, operator needs, and control functions to industrial control panel applications.

Protecting the Operator Interface in Harsh Environments

Front-panel industrial controls form the physical interface between operators and an industrial control system. These controls are subjected to physical contact, repeated actuation, and environmental exposure that can contribute to mechanical wear over time.

Environmental sealing helps protect switches from the dust and water they may encounter at the panel surface. The IP rating system (Figure 1) defined in IEC 60529 classifies protection against the ingress of solids and water under specific standardized test conditions. For example, an IP65 rating indicates a dust-tight enclosure protected against water jets, while an IP67 rating indicates a dust-tight enclosure with protection against temporary immersion in water.[1] Because IP ratings apply only to the specific test conditions defined by the standard, designers should select a rating that aligns with the switch’s expected operating environment.

Figure 1: The numbers in the IP ratings table correlate to the type and amount of protection provided. (Source: Mouser)

Proper sealing extends beyond the switch itself. Panel cutout dimensions, mounting hardware, gasket design, and installation quality all influence how effectively a switch maintains environmental protection at the enclosure boundary. Even small gaps or misaligned sealing components can reduce protection against moisture and particle ingress.

In addition to environmental exposure, switches must also endure the mechanical demands of daily operation. Stainless steel and metal alloy housings can help resist the physical wear from repeated use while protecting the switch from accidental impacts and other physical stress commonly encountered in industrial environments.

Meeting the varying challenges of industrial settings requires designers to balance environmental protection and mechanical durability with usability and system integration.

Designing for Operator Interaction and Panel Integration

There has been a growing emphasis on ruggedized human-machine interfaces (HMIs), placing greater attention on the durability and reliability of front-panel controls.[2] As a result, switch selection is increasingly affected not only by environmental requirements but also by how the switch integrates into the overall control panel and operator interface.

Operators in modern industrial automation environments often need to quickly identify and engage the correct controls while working in demanding industrial environments. Actuator design can help support these tasks. For example, operators can benefit from flat actuators that reduce the risk of accidental activation. In contrast, raised actuators provide greater tactile feedback, making controls easier to locate and operate by touch. LED illumination and emblem markings offer additional visual cues, helping operators quickly distinguish between control functions and interact with equipment more confidently and efficiently.

Designers should consider the switch’s functionality in relation to the intended control behavior. A momentary switch returns to its normal state when released, while a maintained switch stays in its selected state until actuated again. Momentary off-(on) and maintained off-on configurations enable designers to select the behavior that is appropriate for the required control action within the overall system.

Matching Switch Features to Control Panel Requirements

Generally, selecting an anti-vandal switch comes down to matching its features to the application’s requirements. Designers should begin by evaluating the expected operating environment. The switch’s IP rating should align with the panel’s expected exposure to weather, liquids, dust, and particle ingress. From there, designers can consider the housing materials and design based on the application’s mechanical and operational requirements.

After deciding on the type of switch, designers must integrate it into the overall panel design. Selecting a switch with the appropriate cutout and mounting, along with the correct termination and electrical requirements, is necessary to ensure optimal panel integration. Designers should also verify that switch selection aligns with system-level safety and control logic to help ensure safe operation and reliable performance.

The Same Sky Anti-Vandal Switches product line illustrates how these considerations can be combined within a single product family. Available in stainless steel or black metal alloy housings, the switches offer IP65 or IP67-rated protection for rugged operation in harsh environments. Options include multiple voltage ratings and LED-illuminated colors, with optional power emblem markings for simpler operator differentiation and ease of use. The switches are available in 12mm, 16mm, 19mm, and 22mm cutout dimensions, offering flexible panel design and integration options and have an operating temperature range of -20°C to 85°C to provide reliable operation in extreme temperatures. They boast a typical operating force of 450gf to 600gf and offer SPST, SPDT, or SPST-NO circuits with momentary or maintained on/off switch functions, and come with flat or raised actuators.

Conclusion

Anti-vandal switches are a practical option for use in industrial control panels operating in rugged conditions, where durability and reliability are especially important at the point of user interaction. Matching the housing, cutout dimensions, and environmental sealing to the panel’s requirements can help reduce wear over the switch’s life while supporting reliable operation. Options such as different LED colors and actuator styles also give designers greater flexibility to match the interface to the application’s needs.
